## Neighborhoods he works in (each page: satellite map, photos, places, rules, FAQ)

- [Malibu](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/malibu): Twenty-one miles of coast, its own city, and septic tanks. City of Malibu, ZIP 90265.
- [Marina del Rey](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/marina-del-rey): Boats, high-rises and the bike path, run by the county. Unincorporated LA County, ZIP 90292.
- [Pacific Palisades](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/pacific-palisades): A beach town in the hills, rebuilding after the January 2025 fire. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 90272.
- [Playa Vista](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/playa-vista): A planned neighborhood with a park every few blocks. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 90094.
- [Playa del Rey](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/playa-del-rey): The quiet beach town most of LA forgets about. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 90293.
- [Santa Monica](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/santa-monica): The beach city with its own rules, its own schools and a train to Downtown. City of Santa Monica, ZIP 90401, 90402, 90403, 90404, 90405.
- [Venice](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/venice): Abbot Kinney, the canals and the boardwalk, inside the City of LA. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 90291.
- [Brentwood](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/brentwood): Big lots, big trees, and the San Vicente coral trees. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 90049.
- [Century City](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/century-city): High-rise living on the old 20th Century Fox backlot. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 90067.
- [Cheviot Hills & Rancho Park](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/cheviot-hills): Curving streets next to the best public park on the Westside. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 90064.
- [Culver City](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/culver-city): Its own city, its own schools, and a downtown that works. City of Culver City, ZIP 90230, 90232.
- [Mar Vista](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/mar-vista): Westside residential streets and mid-century homes, minutes from the beach. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 90066.
- [Palms](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/palms): Dense, central and close to everything. The Westside's renter neighborhood. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 90034.
- [Pico-Robertson & Beverlywood](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/pico-robertson): Walkable, next to Beverly Hills, anchored by Pico Boulevard. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 90035.
- [West LA & Sawtelle](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/west-la): Sawtelle Japantown and the Westside's best casual food. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 90025.
- [Westchester](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/westchester): Post-war houses, real yards, and LMU on the bluff. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 90045.
- [Westwood](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/westwood): UCLA, Westwood Village and the Wilshire Corridor towers. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 90024.
- [Bel Air](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/bel-air): Gated entrances, estate lots and the biggest houses in LA. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 90077.
- [Beverly Hills](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/beverly-hills): Its own city, its own schools, its own police, and the Flats. City of Beverly Hills, ZIP 90210, 90211, 90212.
- [Beverly Hills Post Office](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/bhpo): A 90210 address in the City of LA. Canyons, views and privacy. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 90210.
- [Hollywood Hills](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/hollywood-hills): City views five minutes from Sunset. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 90068, 90046, 90069.
- [Beverly Grove](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/beverly-grove): Third Street, the Beverly Center and Spanish duplexes on every block. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 90048.
- [Fairfax District](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/fairfax): The Original Farmers Market, The Grove and blocks of Spanish duplexes. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 90036.
- [Hancock Park & Larchmont](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/hancock-park): Old LA mansions, Larchmont Village and the Wilshire Country Club. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 90004, 90020.
- [Hollywood](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/hollywood): Studios, nightlife and the B Line. Live a few blocks off the boulevard. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 90028, 90038.
- [Miracle Mile](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/miracle-mile): Museum Row on Wilshire and the subway underneath it. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 90036.
- [West Hollywood](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/west-hollywood): The Sunset Strip, Santa Monica Boulevard and the Design District in under two square miles. City of West Hollywood, ZIP 90069, 90046, 90048.
- [East Hollywood](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/east-hollywood): Thai Town, Little Armenia and Barnsdall Park, right on the B Line. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 90029.
- [Echo Park](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/echo-park): The lake, Dodger Stadium and hillside homes close to Downtown. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 90026.
- [Los Feliz](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/los-feliz): Griffith Park as a backyard and Vermont Avenue for dinner. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 90027.
- [Silver Lake](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/silver-lake): The reservoir loop, Sunset Junction and modernist houses on the hills. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 90026, 90039.
- [Encino](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/encino): Big lots south of Ventura, condos north of it, and the Sepulveda Basin. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 91316, 91436.
- [North Hollywood](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/north-hollywood): The NoHo Arts District and the end of the B Line. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 91601, 91602, 91605, 91606.
- [Reseda](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/reseda): Big flat lots and some of the most attainable houses in the City of LA. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 91335.
- [Sherman Oaks](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/sherman-oaks): Ventura Boulevard, the Galleria and the 405/101 interchange. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 91403, 91423.
- [Studio City](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/studio-city): The Valley's most walkable stretch of Ventura Boulevard. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 91604.
- [Tarzana](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/tarzana): Named for Tarzan, with hillside homes and room to spread out. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 91356.
- [Valley Village](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/valley-village): Quiet streets between Studio City and NoHo. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 91607.
- [Van Nuys](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/van-nuys): Entry-level houses, real lots and room for an ADU. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 91401, 91405, 91406, 91411.
- [Woodland Hills](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/woodland-hills): Warner Center, Topanga trails and the Valley's west end. City of Los Angeles, ZIP 91364, 91367.

## LA News: the headline for November 2026

- Nithya Raman is elected mayor of Los Angeles: City Councilmember Nithya Raman defeated incumbent Mayor Karen Bass in the Nov. 3 runoff. The Associated Press had Raman at 52.1% to Bass's 47.9% as of Nov. 5, when NBC News projected the win. Bass is the first incumbent LA mayor to lose a re-election bid since 2005. Raman takes office on Dec. 14, 2026.

# Nathaniel Grivas, West Los Angeles REALTOR®

Nathaniel Grivas is a REALTOR® (California DRE #02410660) with The Brodsky Group at Compass Beverly Hills, 9454 Wilshire Blvd, Ste 100, Beverly Hills, CA 90212. Compass is a licensed real estate broker, DRE #01991628.

- Email: nate.grivas@compass.com

## Neighborhood guides

- [Malibu](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/malibu): Twenty-one miles of coast, its own city, and septic tanks.
- [Marina del Rey](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/marina-del-rey): Boats, high-rises and the bike path, run by the county.
- [Pacific Palisades](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/pacific-palisades): A beach town in the hills, rebuilding after the January 2025 fire.
- [Playa Vista](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/playa-vista): A planned neighborhood with a park every few blocks.
- [Playa del Rey](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/playa-del-rey): The quiet beach town most of LA forgets about.
- [Santa Monica](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/santa-monica): The beach city with its own rules, its own schools and a train to Downtown.
- [Venice](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/venice): Abbot Kinney, the canals and the boardwalk, inside the City of LA.
- [Brentwood](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/brentwood): Big lots, big trees, and the San Vicente coral trees.
- [Century City](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/century-city): High-rise living on the old 20th Century Fox backlot.
- [Cheviot Hills & Rancho Park](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/cheviot-hills): Curving streets next to the best public park on the Westside.
- [Culver City](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/culver-city): Its own city, its own schools, and a downtown that works.
- [Mar Vista](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/mar-vista): Westside residential streets and mid-century homes, minutes from the beach.
- [Palms](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/palms): Dense, central and close to everything. The Westside's renter neighborhood.
- [Pico-Robertson & Beverlywood](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/pico-robertson): Walkable, next to Beverly Hills, anchored by Pico Boulevard.
- [West LA & Sawtelle](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/west-la): Sawtelle Japantown and the Westside's best casual food.
- [Westchester](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/westchester): Post-war houses, real yards, and LMU on the bluff.
- [Westwood](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/westwood): UCLA, Westwood Village and the Wilshire Corridor towers.
- [Bel Air](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/bel-air): Gated entrances, estate lots and the biggest houses in LA.
- [Beverly Hills](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/beverly-hills): Its own city, its own schools, its own police, and the Flats.
- [Beverly Hills Post Office](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/bhpo): A 90210 address in the City of LA. Canyons, views and privacy.
- [Hollywood Hills](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/hollywood-hills): City views five minutes from Sunset.
- [Beverly Grove](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/beverly-grove): Third Street, the Beverly Center and Spanish duplexes on every block.
- [Fairfax District](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/fairfax): The Original Farmers Market, The Grove and blocks of Spanish duplexes.
- [Hancock Park & Larchmont](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/hancock-park): Old LA mansions, Larchmont Village and the Wilshire Country Club.
- [Hollywood](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/hollywood): Studios, nightlife and the B Line. Live a few blocks off the boulevard.
- [Miracle Mile](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/miracle-mile): Museum Row on Wilshire and the subway underneath it.
- [West Hollywood](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/west-hollywood): The Sunset Strip, Santa Monica Boulevard and the Design District in under two square miles.
- [East Hollywood](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/east-hollywood): Thai Town, Little Armenia and Barnsdall Park, right on the B Line.
- [Echo Park](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/echo-park): The lake, Dodger Stadium and hillside homes close to Downtown.
- [Los Feliz](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/los-feliz): Griffith Park as a backyard and Vermont Avenue for dinner.
- [Silver Lake](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/silver-lake): The reservoir loop, Sunset Junction and modernist houses on the hills.
- [Encino](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/encino): Big lots south of Ventura, condos north of it, and the Sepulveda Basin.
- [North Hollywood](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/north-hollywood): The NoHo Arts District and the end of the B Line.
- [Reseda](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/reseda): Big flat lots and some of the most attainable houses in the City of LA.
- [Sherman Oaks](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/sherman-oaks): Ventura Boulevard, the Galleria and the 405/101 interchange.
- [Studio City](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/studio-city): The Valley's most walkable stretch of Ventura Boulevard.
- [Tarzana](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/tarzana): Named for Tarzan, with hillside homes and room to spread out.
- [Valley Village](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/valley-village): Quiet streets between Studio City and NoHo.
- [Van Nuys](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/van-nuys): Entry-level houses, real lots and room for an ADU.
- [Woodland Hills](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/woodland-hills): Warner Center, Topanga trails and the Valley's west end.

## Background

Nathaniel was raised between New York and Seattle and moved to Los Angeles for Loyola Marymount University, where he graduated cum laude in Marketing with a minor in Business Law. He worked in marketing at Compass before becoming an agent on The Brodsky Group, and he brings both to every deal: a marketer's eye for how a home is presented and found, and a contract-minded approach to terms, timelines and risk.

## What he does

Pricing and listing preparation, marketing and launch, buyer representation in competitive offers, negotiation through escrow, leasing, and development work: teardown and lot value analysis, zoning and ADU feasibility, and off-market sourcing for builders and investors. When a deal needs a lender, a contractor, an architect, a 1031 intermediary or a tax professional, he brings in the right one.

West Los Angeles, Beverly Hills and the Hills, the beach cities from Malibu to Playa del Rey, Hollywood to Silver Lake, and the San Fernando Valley. Every neighborhood he covers has its own page in [Local LA](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods), with a map of the places locals go.

How it went

## The play: market the land to builders

18748 Lanark is a 21,758 sq ft lot, 72 feet wide and 300 feet deep, zoned RA-1. A 1928 house sits near the street, and about 150 feet of open land runs behind it. The family had owned it since 1994.

The value was in the land, so I marketed it as a land play for builders and developers. I flew drone aerials to show the full depth of the lot, pulled the zoning, and put it in front of investors and the agents who work with them.

It hit the MLS on August 11, 2026 at $999,000. Multiple offers came in the first week, seven by day nine, six of them all cash. On August 20 it went into escrow at $1,200,000.

The buyer's appraisal came back at $1,108,300. I held the price at $1,155,000, $46,700 above the appraisal, and got my sellers a 29-day stay after closing for $1 in rent. It closed on September 25, 2026.

Timeline

- **Aug 11** Listed at $999,000
- **First week** Multiple offers in
- **Aug 20** In escrow at $1,200,000 with 7 offers
- **Aug 27** Appraisal at $1,108,300
- **Sep 8** Price held at $1,155,000
- **Sep 25** Closed at $1,155,000

How it went

## The play: remodel, add two ADUs, rent

My buyer wanted a Valley corner lot with room to build. 14757 Hartland hit the MLS on May 28, 2026 at $825,000: a 1954 three-bedroom, two-bath house with 1,591 sq ft on a 7,119 sq ft corner lot at the start of a cul-de-sac.

The plan is to remodel the front house, add two ADUs in the back and rent them out. The corner lot and the position of the garage leave room behind the house for both units.

The seller had multiple offers. We came in all cash and went into contract on June 2, five days after it listed, at $856,000.

The seller's terms said no repairs and no credits. Our inspections found sewer, foundation, termite and chimney work, so I priced every item from the reports and took it back to the seller. A week into escrow the price came down to $825,000, $31,000 less. It closed on July 13, 2026.

# Malibu

Twenty-one miles of coast, its own city, and septic tanks.

Malibu ZIP 90265 $$$$ · Top of market

Get Malibu listings What's my Malibu home worth?

What it’s like

Life runs along PCH: Point Dume and Zuma in the west, the Malibu Country Mart and Cross Creek in the middle, Carbon Beach and the pier to the east, Pepperdine up on the hill. It's quiet, spread out, and you drive everywhere.

Malibu is its own city stretching along about 21 miles of coastline west of Pacific Palisades. Parts of eastern Malibu burned in the January 2025 Palisades Fire.

The story of Malibu

## The ranch one family fought to keep private

For decades almost all of Malibu belonged to one family. Frederick and May Rindge bought the old Malibu rancho in the 1890s, and after Frederick died, May spent her fortune fighting the railroad, the county and the state to keep everyone else out. She lost, the coast highway opened, and she turned to tiles and movie stars to pay the bills. Malibu became its own city in 1991.

3 min read 9 milestones 3 chapters 4 landmarks

### Timeline

- Chumash era

The village of Humaliwo, usually translated as the place where the surf sounds loudly, gives Malibu its name.

- 1890s

Frederick and May Rindge buy the Malibu rancho, more than 13,000 acres of coast and canyon.

- 1903

The Rindges incorporate their own railroad along the coast so a competing line cannot be built across their land.

- 1905

Frederick dies. May takes over the ranch and the fight to keep it private.

- 1923

The U.S. Supreme Court rules against her in Rindge Co. v. County of Los Angeles, clearing the way for a public road.

- 1926

Short of cash, May founds Malibu Potteries and begins leasing beach lots to movie stars, the start of the Malibu Colony.

- 1929

The Adamson House, covered in Malibu tile, is built for her daughter beside Malibu Lagoon.

- 1932

Malibu Potteries closes after a fire the year before.

- 1991

Malibu incorporates as a city on March 28.

IThe Queen of the Malibu

### May Rindge's war

**13,000+** acres owned by one family

When Frederick Rindge died in 1905, his widow May inherited a ranch that ran for miles along the coast, and she was determined to keep it whole. She posted riders on the boundaries, built a private railroad so the Southern Pacific could not run a line through, and fought the county's plans for a public highway in court for years. In 1923 the U.S. Supreme Court ruled against her, and the coast road, today's Pacific Coast Highway, opened through Malibu by the end of the decade.

IITiles and movie stars

### How Malibu paid its legal bills

**1926** Malibu Potteries opens

The lawsuits left May Rindge land-rich and cash-poor. In 1926 she opened Malibu Potteries near the pier, whose glazed tiles became some of the most prized in California, and she began leasing beach lots to film stars who built cottages there, the start of the Malibu Colony. The pottery burned in 1931 and closed a year later, but the best surviving examples of its work cover the Adamson House, built in 1929 for her daughter Rhoda and now a state historic site.

III1991

### A city of its own

**1991** Malibu incorporates

For most of the twentieth century Malibu was unincorporated county land. Residents voted to form their own city in 1991, largely to control development along the coast. The surf break at Surfrider Beach, which helped launch California surf culture, was named the first World Surfing Reserve in 2010.

Test yourself

01 **Where does the name Malibu come from?** Tap for the answer

From the Chumash village Humaliwo, usually translated as the place where the surf sounds loudly.

02 **Why is there so much colorful tile in the Adamson House?** Tap for the answer

It was built in 1929 by the family that ran Malibu Potteries, and it holds the best surviving collection of Malibu tile.

03 **Who tried to keep the public out of Malibu?** Tap for the answer

May Rindge, who fought a highway through her ranch all the way to the U.S. Supreme Court and lost in 1923.

04 **When did Malibu become a city?** Tap for the answer

March 28, 1991.

## The homes, the rules and who it fits

### The housing

Beachfront, bluff-top and canyon homes, many on large lots. Most of Malibu runs on septic systems instead of sewer, coastal permits add time to projects, and fire insurance is a real line item. Inspect all three before you write an offer.

**Good fit if**

You want privacy, ocean and space, and the drive into town doesn't bother you.

**Think twice if**

You want walkability or a short commute anywhere.

Run the numbers [Mortgage](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/mortgage) [Rent vs buy](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/rent-vs-buy) [Transfer tax](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/transfer-tax/?city=malibu) [Compare](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/compare/?a=malibu&b=pacific-palisades)

The rules here

- **Jurisdiction:** City of Malibu
- **Transfer tax:** 0.11% county only
- **Measure ULA:** No No
- **Rent control:** No local rent control. California's statewide cap (AB 1482) covers eligible rentals
- **Public schools:** Santa Monica-Malibu Unified, with a separate Malibu Unified in the works

What is Malibu like?

Is Malibu its own city?

Malibu is in City of Malibu. It sets its own taxes, rules and services.

What ZIP codes cover Malibu?

Malibu is mostly ZIP 90265.

What kind of homes are in Malibu?

Beachfront, bluff-top and canyon homes, many on large lots. Most of Malibu runs on septic systems instead of sewer, coastal permits add time to projects, and fire insurance is a real line item. Inspect all three before you write an offer.

0.11% county only

Does rent control apply in Malibu?

No local rent control. California's statewide cap (AB 1482) covers eligible rentals

# Marina del Rey

Boats, high-rises and the bike path, run by the county.

LA County ZIP 90292 $$$ · Upper

Get Marina del Rey listings What's my Marina del Rey home worth?

What it’s like

Life here runs around the water: paddleboarding in the harbor, calm water at Mother's Beach, the bike path to Venice and Playa del Rey, and sunset walks along the main channel.

Marina del Rey is unincorporated LA County, built around a small-craft harbor that opened in the 1960s. The county owns most of the land, so most buildings sit on long-term ground leases.

The story of Marina del Rey

## From salt marsh to the biggest small-craft harbor in North America

For most of a century, people tried to put a harbor in the Ballona marsh and failed. In the 1950s Los Angeles County finally built one for pleasure boats instead of ships, and when Marina del Rey was dedicated in 1965 it was the largest man-made small-craft harbor in the world. Almost all of it still sits on county land.

3 min read 8 milestones 3 chapters 4 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1839

Rancho La Ballona is granted to the Machado and Talamantes families.

- 1887

Investors dredge a small harbor called Port Ballona. It silts up and fails.

- 1916

The Army Corps of Engineers calls a big commercial port here impractical and suggests a small-craft harbor.

- 1949

The Corps proposes a full plan for a marina.

- 1956

County voters approve $13 million in revenue bonds to help pay for it.

- 1957

Ground is broken on December 12.

- 1962

The first boaters arrive in Basin B, and a winter storm soon damages the harbor.

- 1965

Marina del Rey is formally dedicated on April 10. Total cost: $36.25 million.

IBallona

### The harbor that kept failing

**1887** Port Ballona, the first try

Before the boats, this was a salt marsh fed by Ballona Creek. In 1887 investors dredged a little harbor they called Port Ballona, and the sand closed it up. When Los Angeles went looking for a deepwater port, the federal government picked San Pedro. In 1916 the Army Corps of Engineers decided a big commercial port here would never work, but floated the idea of a harbor for small boats.

II1957 to 1965

### Building the marina

**~5,000** boat slips

It took four decades for that idea to get funded. County voters approved revenue bonds in 1956, ground was broken in 1957, and crews turned roughly 800 acres of marsh into seven basins. Architect Victor Gruen drew the master plan. The first boats tied up in 1962, a winter storm battered the unfinished breakwater, and the county added a new one before the formal dedication on April 10, 1965. Today the harbor holds roughly 5,000 boats.

IIIFor buyers

### A town on leased land

**County** owns most of the land

Marina del Rey is not a city. It is unincorporated Los Angeles County, and the county owns most of the land, leasing parcels to developers who built the apartments, condos, hotels and restaurants. That is why many condos here are sold on long-term ground leases rather than as fee simple property, a detail every buyer should understand before making an offer.

Test yourself

### Did you know?

01 **Is Marina del Rey part of the City of Los Angeles?** Tap for the answer

No. It is unincorporated Los Angeles County, and the county owns most of the land.

02 **How big is the harbor?** Tap for the answer

About 800 acres, roughly half of it water, with slips for about 5,000 boats.

03 **When did it open?** Tap for the answer

The first boats arrived in 1962, and the harbor was formally dedicated on April 10, 1965.

## The homes, the rules and who it fits

### The housing

Mostly apartments and condo towers. Many condos are leasehold, so the length of the ground lease affects financing and value. Ask about the lease term before you fall in love with the view.

**Good fit if**

You want water views, the bike path and an easy condo lifestyle.

**Think twice if**

You want to own your land outright or have a yard.

- **Transfer tax:** 0.11% county only

Weather

### Record king tides and big surf hit the coast on Thanksgiving morning

An extreme high tide of about 8 feet arrived Thursday morning, with a coastal flood advisory for the Malibu coast and LA County beaches through noon and a high surf warning until 9 p.m. Forecasters expect waves of roughly 6 to 11 feet with strong rip currents, and the LA Harbor tied its all-time high-water mark. If you're heading to the beach this weekend, check tide times before parking in beach lots and stay off the rocks and jetties.

# Pacific Palisades, Los Angeles: History, Landmarks, Map & Where to Eat | Local LA

# Pacific Palisades

A beach town in the hills, rebuilding after the January 2025 fire.

City of LA ZIP 90272 $$$$ · Top of market

Get Pacific Palisades listings What's my Pacific Palisades home worth?

What it’s like

Before the fire it was the Westside's small town: a village center, canyon trails and beaches below the bluffs. Neighborhoods include the Alphabet Streets, the Huntington, the Riviera, the Highlands and Castellammare. Temescal Canyon and Topanga State Park trails start here.

Pacific Palisades is part of the City of LA, between Santa Monica and Malibu. The January 2025 Palisades Fire destroyed thousands of homes here, and much of the community is now in rebuild.

Block by block

## The pockets of Pacific Palisades

[Every LA pocket on one map →](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/map)

In Los Angeles a single street can change the price of a house. Pacific Palisades is really 14 smaller neighborhoods, and these are the lines between them, drawn street by street. Dashed outlines are the pockets next door.

### Castellammare

The hillside above Pacific Coast Highway where Sunset meets the coast

Italian-named streets stacked on the bluff above PCH, with Mediterranean villas and ocean views from almost every lot. Much of it is rebuilding after the 2025 fire.

### Paseo Miramar

Paseo Miramar and the streets off it, above Sunset near PCH

A steep hillside enclave reached by one winding road, with big ocean and canyon views and a trailhead to Parker Mesa at the top.

### Palisades Highlands

Palisades Drive north of Sunset, up Santa Ynez Canyon

A planned 1970s and 80s community up Santa Ynez Canyon, with newer homes, townhouses and gated enclaves surrounded by Topanga State Park.

### Marquez Knolls

North of Sunset between El Medio and Palisades Drive

Postwar ranch houses and newer view homes on the slope above Sunset, with a small shopping strip at Marquez Avenue and ocean views on many streets. Much of it is rebuilding after the 2025 fire.

### Upper Bienveneda & El Medio

North of Sunset between Marquez Knolls and Temescal Canyon

Hillside streets off Bienveneda and upper El Medio with some of the biggest ocean views in the Palisades, just above Palisades Charter High School.

### Alphabet Streets

North of Sunset, east of the Village, below Temescal Gateway Park

The original 1920s Palisades, laid out on streets named alphabetically for Methodist missionaries. Narrow streets and small lots, walkable to the Village, and rebuilding after the 2025 fire.

### Upper Riviera

North of Sunset around Amalfi Drive

Winding streets above the Riviera Country Club with large hillside lots, privacy and canyon views, bordering Brentwood and Will Rogers State Historic Park.

### El Medio Bluffs

South of Sunset from Temescal Canyon west to Las Casas

A mesa of single-family homes on the bluff above PCH, with ocean views along the rim streets.

### Via Bluffs

South of Sunset between Temescal Canyon and Potrero Canyon

Bluff-top streets named for colleges, a short walk south of the Village, with ocean views along the edge.

### The Village

Sunset Boulevard's commercial core around Swarthmore and Via de la Paz

The Palisades' downtown: Palisades Village shops, the Village Green and a grid of homes and condos within walking distance of everything.

### The Huntington

South of Sunset between Potrero Canyon and Chautauqua Boulevard

Wide, walkable streets of large homes on the bluff, close to the Village and the beach. One of the most sought-after pockets on the Westside.

### Lower Riviera

South of Sunset around the Riviera Country Club

Large homes on Napoli Drive and the streets ringing the Riviera golf course, where the Napoli rim lots look straight over the fairways.

### Rustic Canyon

The canyon floor along Latimer and Brooktree roads

A wooded creek canyon of rustic homes and sycamores around Rustic Canyon Park, hidden below Sunset.

### Santa Monica Canyon

Entrada Drive, Channel Road and the canyon streets above the beach

A canyon pocket a block from the sand, with Channel Road's restaurants, older beach cottages and hillside homes, all in the City of LA.

The story of Pacific Palisades

## A Methodist utopia, a movie ranch and a haven for exiles

Pacific Palisades was founded by ministers who wanted a town of lectures, churches and clean living above the sea. Before them came a silent-film studio and a rancho; after them came a cowboy star's ranch, a colony of European writers fleeing the Nazis, and some of the most important modern houses in America. In January 2025 most of it burned, and the town is now rebuilding for the second century it had only just begun.

4 min read 11 milestones 4 chapters 6 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1838

The land is granted to Francisco Marquez and Ysidro Reyes as part of Rancho Boca de Santa Monica.

- 1911

Director Thomas Ince builds Inceville, a Western movie studio, at Sunset and the coast.

- 1922

On January 14, Rev. Charles H. Scott and the founders draw lots for home sites under the oaks of Temescal Canyon.

- 1926

Will Rogers buys his ranch in upper Rustic Canyon, with a polo field he plays on with Hollywood friends.

- 1927

The Riviera Country Club opens. Ben Hogan wins the 1948 U.S. Open there.

- 1940s

Thomas Mann, Lion Feuchtwanger and other exiled European writers settle here, a community nicknamed Weimar on the Pacific.

- 1949

Charles and Ray Eames finish their steel-and-glass house, Case Study House No. 8.

- 1950

The Self-Realization Fellowship Lake Shrine opens off Sunset Boulevard.

- 1974

J. Paul Getty's museum opens in a re-created Roman villa above the coast, today's Getty Villa.

- 2025

On January 7, the Palisades Fire burns 23,448 acres and destroys 6,837 structures. Twelve people die.

- 2028

Riviera is scheduled to host golf at the Los Angeles Olympics.

IFounders Day

### A town planned by ministers

**1922** founders draw lots in Temescal Canyon

Before the town, the coast below the bluffs belonged to the movies. In 1911 Thomas Ince built Inceville, a sprawling Western studio where Sunset Boulevard meets the sea, and the canyons served as backlots for a decade.

In 1922 the Rev. Charles H. Scott and a Methodist association bought the land for a Chautauqua-style community: churches, lecture halls, summer assemblies and a quiet, sober town on the cliffs. On January 14, 1922, the founders gathered under the oaks in Temescal Canyon and drew lots for their home sites. Early streets were named for Methodist leaders, and Temescal Gateway Park still occupies the old assembly grounds.

IIRustic Canyon

### Will Rogers and the polo crowd

**31** rooms in the Will Rogers ranch house

In 1926 Will Rogers, then one of the most popular entertainers in America, bought land in upper Rustic Canyon and built a ranch with a 31-room house, stables, a roping arena and a regulation polo field where he played with friends from the studios. After he died in a plane crash in 1935, his family gave the ranch to the state, and it is now Will Rogers State Historic Park, with polo still played on the field.

The canyon below had its own society. The Uplifters, a club spun off from the Los Angeles Athletic Club, built rustic weekend cabins under the sycamores of Rustic Canyon in the 1920s.

IIIWeimar on the Pacific

### Exiles, modernists and a museum

**1949** the Eames House is finished

In the 1930s and 1940s, writers, composers and artists fleeing Hitler found refuge in the Palisades. Novelist Thomas Mann built a house on San Remo Drive, Lion Feuchtwanger lived at Villa Aurora above the coast, and the community they formed became known as Weimar on the Pacific. Villa Aurora later became a residence for visiting artists.

After the war the Palisades became a laboratory for modern architecture. In 1949 Charles and Ray Eames finished their house and studio on the bluff above Chautauqua Boulevard, Case Study House No. 8, built from off-the-shelf steel parts. The Lake Shrine, a spiritual garden around a spring-fed lake, opened in 1950, and in 1974 J. Paul Getty opened his antiquities museum in a re-created Roman villa, today's Getty Villa.

IV2025

### The fire and the rebuild

**6,837** structures destroyed in the Palisades Fire

On January 7, 2025, the Palisades Fire broke out during a severe Santa Ana windstorm. Over the following weeks it burned 23,448 acres and destroyed 6,837 structures, most of them homes, across the Palisades and into Malibu, and 12 people died. It was the most destructive fire in the city's history.

Rebuilding is now the defining story of the Palisades. Lots are being cleared, permits issued and new homes framed street by street, and many buyers and sellers here are working through insurance, rebuild costs and new fire-safety rules at the same time. In November 2026 a federal jury convicted the man charged with starting the fire that prosecutors say rekindled into the Palisades Fire.

### Did you know?

01 **Who founded Pacific Palisades?** Tap for the answer

A Methodist association led by the Rev. Charles H. Scott, which bought the land in 1922 for a Chautauqua-style community of churches and lecture halls.

02 **Is polo still played at Will Rogers' ranch?** Tap for the answer

Yes. The regulation field he built in the 1920s is still used, and the ranch is now Will Rogers State Historic Park.

03 **What was Weimar on the Pacific?** Tap for the answer

The community of German and Austrian writers and artists, including Thomas Mann and Lion Feuchtwanger, who settled here in exile in the 1930s and 1940s.

04 **Where will golf be played at the 2028 Olympics?** Tap for the answer

At the Riviera Country Club in the Palisades, where Ben Hogan won the 1948 U.S. Open.

Single-family homes and estates, with many lots now in rebuild. Buyers are looking at lots, rebuild plans and permits. In November 2026, LA voters approved Proposition TE, which exempts many fire-damaged homes sold by their January 2025 owners within five years from the ULA tax.

What it’s like

Everything is new and close: Runway for shopping and dinner, Central Park with a pool and courts, dozens of pocket parks, and the Ballona Wetlands next door. Very stroller friendly.

Playa Vista was built from scratch starting in the early 2000s on the former Hughes Aircraft site, where Howard Hughes built the Spruce Goose. The hangar is now office space, and tech campuses fill the area.

The story of Playa Vista

## Where Howard Hughes built the Spruce Goose

Playa Vista sits at the edge of the Ballona Wetlands, on the land where Howard Hughes built his aircraft company, one of the longest private runways in the country and the largest wooden airplane ever flown. After decades of fights over what should replace it, a planned community rose here starting in 2002, and the old hangars now house studios and tech companies.

3 min read 8 milestones 3 chapters 3 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1940

Howard Hughes buys 380 acres below the Westchester bluffs for about $500,000.

- 1941

The Hughes Aircraft plant is fully running.

- 1943

Hughes builds a runway nearly 9,600 feet long, among the longest private runways anywhere.

- 1940s

The H-4 Hercules, nicknamed the Spruce Goose, is built here in a hangar made of wood because metal was scarce in wartime.

- 1947

The Hercules flies once, briefly, in Long Beach Harbor on November 2.

- 1976

Hughes dies, and the campus is later sold.

- 1985

Hughes Airport closes.

- 2002

Construction of the Playa Vista planned community begins.

IHughes country

### An aircraft empire in a marsh

**380** acres Hughes bought in 1940

In 1940 Howard Hughes bought 380 acres of the Ballona marsh at the foot of the Westchester bluffs and moved his young aircraft company here. He built factories, a private airfield and a runway nearly 9,600 feet long, and for four decades the site produced aircraft, radar, weapons systems and experimental helicopters.

IIThe Hercules

### The Spruce Goose

**319 ft 11 in** wingspan, still the largest of any plane

During the war Hughes was hired to build a giant flying boat to carry troops over the Atlantic. Because aluminum was rationed, both the plane and the hangar it was built in were made of wood. The H-4 Hercules, which Hughes hated hearing called the Spruce Goose, was moved in sections to Long Beach and flew exactly once, on November 2, 1947. Its wingspan, nearly 320 feet, is still the largest of any aircraft ever built. The plane now sits in a museum in Oregon, but the wooden hangar still stands.

IIISilicon Beach

### From runway to neighborhood

**2002** Playa Vista breaks ground

After the airport closed in 1985, developers, environmental groups and the city spent years fighting over the land. The compromise created Playa Vista, a planned neighborhood with parks every few blocks, and restored part of the Ballona wetlands next door. The Hughes hangars became sound stages and offices, and the area's tech tenants helped earn the Westside its Silicon Beach nickname.

Test yourself

### Did you know?

01 **Is the Spruce Goose made of spruce?** Tap for the answer

Mostly not. It is built largely of birch, and Hughes disliked the nickname.

02 **Where is the Spruce Goose now?** Tap for the answer

At the Evergreen Aviation and Space Museum in Oregon. Its original hangar still stands in Playa Vista.

03 **How many times did it fly?** Tap for the answer

Once, on November 2, 1947, for about a mile over Long Beach Harbor.

## The homes, the rules and who it fits

### The housing

Newer condos, townhomes and some single-family homes. HOA dues are standard here, and many homes carry special assessments on the tax bill, so read the bill before you compare prices with older neighborhoods.

**Good fit if**

You want new construction, parks and a short walk to work.

**Think twice if**

You want character, older architecture or no HOA.

What it’s like

It feels like a beach town from a few decades ago: a short strip of bars and restaurants on Culver Boulevard, Del Rey Lagoon park, and Dockweiler's fire rings at night. The south end sits under the LAX flight path.

The story of Playa del Rey

## A lagoon resort and the town the airport erased

Playa del Rey opened in 1902 as a seaside resort on a lagoon, with a pavilion, a hotel and a pier, and buyers rode out by streetcar. In the 1920s developers pushed it south along the dunes. Then the jets came. By the mid-1970s the airport had bought and cleared the neighborhood called Surfridge, and its empty streets became a refuge for an endangered butterfly.

3 min read 8 milestones 2 chapters 4 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1880s

Investors try and fail to build a harbor called Port Ballona at the mouth of Ballona Creek.

- 1902

The Playa del Rey resort opens. Buyers ride a streetcar to Alla station, where horse-drawn coaches meet them.

- 1900s

A pavilion, the Del Rey Hotel and a pier rise around the lagoon.

- 1920s

Developers Dickinson and Gillespie extend the town south along the dunes as Palisades del Rey, including Surfridge.

- 1928

Mines Field, the future LAX, opens just inland.

- 1960s

Jet traffic makes the dunes neighborhood nearly unlivable.

- 1970s

The airport buys out and removes roughly 800 homes in Surfridge.

- Today

The cleared dunes are a protected habitat for the El Segundo blue butterfly.

I1902

### The resort on the lagoon

**1902** the resort opens

Playa del Rey began as a getaway. In 1902 buyers were sent by streetcar to Alla station and carried the rest of the way by coach to a new resort on the lagoon, with a pavilion, a hotel and a pier. The lagoon survives as Del Rey Lagoon Park, the quiet heart of the neighborhood.

IISurfridge

### The neighborhood LAX erased

**~800** homes removed

In the 1920s the town grew south along the bluffs and dunes as Palisades del Rey, and its southern section, Surfridge, became a fashionable beach colony with sweeping ocean views. The airport inland grew too. When jets arrived, the noise over Surfridge became unbearable, and in the 1960s and 1970s the airport bought the homes and moved or demolished them.

The streets were left behind. Today you can still see the old roads and curbs behind the fences west of LAX, and the dunes have been replanted with the buckwheat that the endangered El Segundo blue butterfly needs. The ghost town is now one of the largest refuges for the species.

Test yourself

### Did you know?

01 **What happened to Surfridge?** Tap for the answer

The airport bought and cleared its roughly 800 homes because of jet noise. The empty streets are still visible behind fences west of LAX.

02 **What lives in the LAX dunes now?** Tap for the answer

The endangered El Segundo blue butterfly, which depends on seacliff buckwheat growing in the restored dunes.

03 **How did early buyers get to Playa del Rey?** Tap for the answer

By streetcar to Alla station, then by horse-drawn coach to the lagoon.

### Record king tides and big surf hit the coast on Thanksgiving morning

An extreme high tide of about 8 feet arrived Thursday morning, with a coastal flood advisory for the Malibu coast and LA County beaches through noon and a high surf warning until 9 p.m. Forecasters expect waves of roughly 6 to 11 feet with strong rip currents, and the LA Harbor tied its all-time high-water mark. If you're heading to the beach this weekend, check tide times before parking in beach lots and stay off the rocks and jetties.

# Santa Monica, Los Angeles: Best Restaurants, Bars, Things to Do & Map | Local LA

Source page: https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/santa-monica

# Santa Monica

The beach city with its own rules, its own schools and a train to Downtown.

Santa Monica ZIP 90401, 90402, 90403, 90404, 90405 $$$$ · Top of market

Get Santa Monica listings What's my Santa Monica home worth?

What it’s like

North of Montana Avenue is the quiet, polished side: wide streets, big trees and Montana's boutiques and coffee. Downtown has the Third Street Promenade, the Pier and the Metro E Line terminal at 4th and Colorado. Main Street and Ocean Park to the south feel looser and closer to Venice.

Santa Monica is its own city, about eight square miles of bluffs and flats between Pacific Palisades, Brentwood and Venice. It runs its own transfer tax, rent control and school district, so the rules change the second you cross the city line.

Block by block

## The pockets of Santa Monica

[Every LA pocket on one map →](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/map)

In Los Angeles a single street can change the price of a house. Santa Monica is really 9 smaller neighborhoods, and these are the lines between them, drawn street by street. Dashed outlines are the pockets next door.

### North of Montana

Montana Avenue north to the city line at the canyon rim, Ocean Avenue to 26th Street

Santa Monica's estate grid: wide, tree-lined numbered streets of large single-family homes, with Montana Avenue's shops at the bottom and San Vicente's coral-tree median running through. It is the only Santa Monica neighborhood with its own private patrol.

### Gold Coast

The beachfront strip along Palisades Beach Road, below the Palisades Park bluffs

A single row of houses on the sand north of the pier, many dating to the studio era of the 1920s and 30s. Lots back straight onto the beach, with the Annenberg Community Beach House in the middle.

### Wilshire Montana

Wilshire Boulevard to Montana Avenue, Ocean Avenue to 26th Street

Condos and small apartment buildings near the ocean that give way to single-family streets as you head east toward 26th. Walkable to Montana Avenue, Wilshire and Downtown.

### Northeast Santa Monica

Wilshire Boulevard to Montana Avenue east of 26th Street, to the Los Angeles line

A small, quiet pocket of single-family homes and low-rise condos on the Brentwood border, with Santa Monica schools and city services.

### Downtown Santa Monica

Ocean Avenue to Lincoln Boulevard, Wilshire Boulevard to Pico Boulevard

The Third Street Promenade, the pier, the Expo line terminus and the Civic Center. Mostly condos, lofts and rentals, a few blocks from the sand.

### Mid-City

Lincoln Boulevard to the city line, Wilshire Boulevard to Olympic Boulevard

Santa Monica's medical and commercial middle, with both of the city's hospitals and a mix of condos, apartments and single-family streets.

### Pico Neighborhood

Olympic Boulevard to Pico Boulevard, Lincoln Boulevard to Centinela Avenue

Virginia Avenue Park and the Bergamot arts district anchor this mixed pocket of bungalows, duplexes and apartments between the freeway and Pico.

### Ocean Park

Pico Boulevard to the Venice line, the beach to Lincoln Boulevard

Main Street's shops, Ocean Park Boulevard and walk-street cottages near the sand. Small lots, Craftsman bungalows and modern rebuilds sit side by side.

### Sunset Park

Pico Boulevard to the city line, Lincoln Boulevard east to the airport

Santa Monica's family pocket: blocks of 1940s and 50s single-family homes around Clover Park and the airport, with Ocean Park Boulevard's cafes and Santa Monica schools.

- 4 **Metro E Line** Downtown Santa Monica station connects to Culver City and Downtown LA.
- 5 **The beach bike path** The Marvin Braude trail runs south through Venice and beyond.

Santa Monica is a beach city with its own rules and a deep bench of restaurants, from a 1950s seaside shack to tasting menus that book a month out. Main Street and Ocean Park are the relaxed half; downtown, Wilshire and Montana carry the rest.

The story of Santa Monica

## The city on the sea that almost became LA's port

Santa Monica was laid out in 1875 by a silver-rich senator who wanted a seaport. It lost the harbor fight to San Pedro and became a beach town instead, and along the way it built California's oldest pleasure pier, launched the first flight around the world and became the end of the most famous highway in America.

3 min read 10 milestones 3 chapters 4 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1839

Rancho San Vicente y Santa Monica is granted to the Sepulveda family.

- 1872

Col. Robert S. Baker buys 38,409 acres of the rancho for $54,000.

- 1875

Baker and Nevada Senator John P. Jones lay out the town and hold the first land sale on July 10.

- 1886

Santa Monica incorporates as a city.

- 1890s

The Long Wharf, nearly a mile out into the bay, makes Santa Monica a contender to be the port of Los Angeles. Federal harbor money goes to San Pedro instead.

- 1909

The Municipal Pier is built, first to carry a sewage pipe past the surf.

- 1916

Charles Looff builds the pleasure pier next door and the Hippodrome to house its carousel.

- 1922

Donald Douglas opens an aircraft plant at Clover Field.

- 1924

Douglas World Cruisers take off from Clover Field. Two finish the first flight around the world, landing home on September 23 to a crowd of about 200,000.

- 1943

Douglas employs as many as 44,000 people building wartime aircraft.

ICity on the sea

### A port that wasn't

**1875** the first land sale, July 10

Santa Monica began as a business plan. Col. Robert Baker bought most of the old Sepulveda rancho in 1872, and Senator John P. Jones, rich from Nevada silver, bought in two years later. They laid out a town in 1875, set aside the bluff-top park now called Palisades Park, and planned a seaport that would make it the gateway to Los Angeles.

For a while it looked possible. Southern Pacific built the Long Wharf near the mouth of Santa Monica Canyon in the 1890s and ran trains out over the water. But the fight over where the federal government would build LA's harbor went to San Pedro in 1897, and Santa Monica turned to what it does best: sun, sand and visitors.

IIThe pier

### A sewage pipe that became a landmark

**1909** California's oldest pleasure pier

The pier that defines the city was built in 1909 to carry a sewage line out to sea, and anglers took it over almost immediately. In 1916 amusement builder Charles Looff, who had built Coney Island's first carousel, added a pleasure pier beside it with rides and the Hippodrome, an exotic building made to hold a carousel. The Hippodrome still turns one today.

IIIWings

### The first flight around the world

**200,000** people at Clover Field to welcome the fliers home

In 1922 Donald Douglas set up an aircraft factory at Clover Field, today's Santa Monica Airport. Two years later four of his Douglas World Cruisers took off to try to circle the globe. Two made it, covering more than 27,000 miles in 175 days, and came home on September 23, 1924 to a crowd of about 200,000. During the Second World War the Douglas plant employed as many as 44,000 people, and its workers filled the bungalows and apartments that still line the city's side streets.

## The homes, the rules and who it fits

### The housing

North of Montana is single-family and some of the most expensive streets on the Westside. Between Montana and Wilshire and through Mid-City you get condos, duplexes and older apartment buildings. Sunset Park and Ocean Park have smaller houses and bungalows. Much of the older apartment stock falls under Santa Monica rent control.

**Good fit if**

You want the beach, walkability and a train line, and you're fine paying for all three.

**Think twice if**

You want the most space for the money, or you don't want summer beach traffic near your street.

Run the numbers [Mortgage](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/mortgage) [Rent vs buy](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/rent-vs-buy) [Transfer tax](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/transfer-tax/?city=santa-monica) [Compare](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/compare/?a=santa-monica&b=venice)

The rules here

- **Jurisdiction:** City of Santa Monica
- **Transfer tax:** City tax on the full price: 0.3% under $5M, 0.6% from $5M, 5.6% at $8M and up, plus 0.11% county
- **Measure ULA:** No No. Santa Monica has its own top tier instead (5.6% at $8M+)
- **Rent control:** Santa Monica rent control covers most apartments built before April 10, 1979
- **Public schools:** Santa Monica-Malibu Unified (SMMUSD)

### Record king tides and big surf hit the coast on Thanksgiving morning

An extreme high tide of about 8 feet arrived Thursday morning, with a coastal flood advisory for the Malibu coast and LA County beaches through noon and a high surf warning until 9 p.m. Forecasters expect waves of roughly 6 to 11 feet with strong rip currents, and the LA Harbor tied its all-time high-water mark. If you're heading to the beach this weekend, check tide times before parking in beach lots and stay off the rocks and jetties.

Who is a real estate agent who works in Santa Monica?

Nathaniel Grivas, REALTOR® (DRE #02410660) with The Brodsky Group at Compass Beverly Hills, helps people buy, sell, rent, invest and build in Santa Monica and across West LA, Beverly Hills and the San Fernando Valley. Call or text 310-269-5541.

What is Santa Monica like?

North of Montana Avenue is the quiet, polished side: wide streets, big trees and Montana's boutiques and coffee. Downtown has the Third Street Promenade, the Pier and the Metro E Line terminal at 4th and Colorado. Main Street and Ocean Park to the south feel looser and closer to Venice.

Is Santa Monica its own city?

Santa Monica is in City of Santa Monica. It sets its own taxes, rules and services.

What ZIP codes cover Santa Monica?

Santa Monica is mostly ZIP 90401, 90402, 90403, 90404, 90405.

What kind of homes are in Santa Monica?

North of Montana is single-family and some of the most expensive streets on the Westside. Between Montana and Wilshire and through Mid-City you get condos, duplexes and older apartment buildings. Sunset Park and Ocean Park have smaller houses and bungalows. Much of the older apartment stock falls under Santa Monica rent control.

What is the transfer tax when you sell in Santa Monica?

City tax on the full price: 0.3% under $5M, 0.6% from $5M, 5.6% at $8M and up, plus 0.11% county

Does rent control apply in Santa Monica?

Santa Monica rent control covers most apartments built before April 10, 1979

Which public schools serve Santa Monica?

Santa Monica-Malibu Unified (SMMUSD)

# Venice

Abbot Kinney, the canals and the boardwalk, inside the City of LA.

City of LA ZIP 90291 $$$ · Upper

Get Venice listings What's my Venice home worth?

What it’s like

Abbot Kinney Boulevard is the dinner-and-shopping strip. Ocean Front Walk, the skate park and the outdoor courts are the loud, famous part. A few blocks inland the streets go quiet, and the canals are some of the most peaceful blocks in the city.

Venice is part of the City of Los Angeles, between Santa Monica and Marina del Rey. Abbot Kinney built it in 1905 as Venice of America, and LA annexed it in 1926.

[Beach](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/#beach) [Walkable](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/#walkable) [Creative](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/#creative) [Nightlife](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/#nightlife)

Block by block

## The pockets of Venice

[Every LA pocket on one map →](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/map)

In Los Angeles a single street can change the price of a house. Venice is really 8 smaller neighborhoods, and these are the lines between them, drawn street by street. Dashed outlines are the pockets next door.

### Ocean Front Walk

The beach to Pacific Avenue and Main Street, Venice Boulevard to the Santa Monica line

Venice's Ocean Front Walk and the walk streets: beach-close homes and buildings, many on car-free walk streets.

### Oakwood West & North of Rose

Main Street and Abbot Kinney to 6th Avenue, California Avenue to the Santa Monica line

North Venice between Main and Sixth: small lots of cottages, remodels and modern new builds near Rose Avenue.

### Oakwood

6th Avenue to Lincoln Boulevard, California Avenue to the Santa Monica line

Oakwood: Venice's historic working neighborhood, now a mix of original bungalows and new modern homes.

### Windward Circle

Pacific Avenue to Abbot Kinney, Brooks Avenue to Venice Boulevard

Windward Circle and the blocks around it: walk streets and homes between the beach and Abbot Kinney.

### Canals & Silver Triangle

Pacific Avenue to Abbot Kinney, Venice Boulevard to Washington

The Venice Canals: homes facing the six canals and footbridges, plus the streets around them.

### Milwood & Presidents Row

Abbot Kinney to Lincoln, California Avenue to Washington

Milwood: a quiet residential grid off Abbot Kinney of cottages and new builds.

### Penmar (East Venice North)

Lincoln Boulevard to Walgrove, Superba Avenue to the Santa Monica line

Penmar: Venice east of Lincoln near Penmar Park and golf course, with larger lots than west Venice.

### East Venice South

Lincoln Boulevard to Walgrove, Venice Boulevard to Superba

East Venice south of Superba: single-family streets.

## Where to eat, drink and go in Venice

See them on the map →

Venice packs a beach town, one of LA's best restaurant streets and a handful of genuinely odd landmarks into a couple of square miles. Abbot Kinney and Rose Avenue carry most of the eating and drinking; the boardwalk, canals and skatepark carry the rest.

$

56 Windward Ave

A tiny espresso bar a few steps off the boardwalk. People describe it as a friendly escape from the crowds, and the weekend line regularly spills onto the sidewalk.

**Order:** Any espresso drink to go before a walk on the boardwalk.

The story of Venice

## Abbot Kinney's Venice of America

Tobacco millionaire Abbot Kinney opened Venice of America on July 4, 1905, with canals, gondolas, an arcaded main street and an amusement pier. The resort town joined Los Angeles in 1926, most of its canals were paved over three years later, and the rest of the century turned it into the home of bodybuilding, skateboarding and street art.

3 min read 8 milestones 3 chapters 4 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1905

Abbot Kinney opens Venice of America on July 4, with canals dug through the marsh and gondolas on the water.

- 1920

Kinney dies. His resort is already a full town.

- 1926

Venice votes to join Los Angeles, largely for city services.

- 1929

Most of the canals are filled and paved into streets, and oil is struck nearby on the Venice peninsula.

- 1965

Gold's Gym opens in Venice and helps make the beach the center of bodybuilding.

- 1970s

The Zephyr skate team turns drained pools and the boardwalk into the birthplace of modern skateboarding.

- 1982

The surviving canals are listed as a historic district.

- 1990s

The remaining canals are dredged and rebuilt with new walkways and banks.

I1905

### A Venice in California

**July 4, 1905** Venice of America opens

Abbot Kinney made his money in cigarettes and spent it on an idea: a cultural resort by the sea modeled on Venice, Italy. He dug canals through the coastal marsh, brought in gondolas, built Windward Avenue with Italian-style arcades and opened the whole thing on July 4, 1905. Lectures and concerts were the plan. Crowds came for the amusement pier, the rides and the beach.

The colonnades on Windward Avenue and the Venice sign above it are the most visible pieces of Kinney's town that survive.

II1929

### Canals into streets

**1929** most canals paved over

After Venice joined Los Angeles in 1926, the city decided cars mattered more than canals. In 1929 most of them were filled and paved, which is why some Venice streets are unusually wide or curve oddly: they follow old waterways. The same year oil was struck on the peninsula, and derricks rose near the beach. The handful of canals that survived south of Venice Boulevard were restored in the 1990s and are now one of the most photographed residential streets in the city.

IIIThe boardwalk

### Muscle, skate and murals

**1965** Gold's Gym opens

The beach gave Venice its second life. Bodybuilders made the outdoor weight pen famous, and Gold's Gym opened in 1965. In the 1970s the Zephyr team of surf-skaters from the neighborhood known as Dogtown changed skateboarding by riding empty backyard pools. Murals spread across walls up and down the boardwalk, and today the skatepark on the sand is a direct descendant of that era.

## The homes, the rules and who it fits

### The housing

Small lots, walk streets where homes face a pedestrian path, 1920s cottages next to architect-built modern homes. Venice sits in the Coastal Zone, so many projects need a Coastal Development Permit on top of regular permits.

**Good fit if**

You want to walk to the beach and to dinner, and you like energy around you.

**Think twice if**

You want quiet weekends or a big yard.

Run the numbers [Mortgage](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/mortgage) [Rent vs buy](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/rent-vs-buy) [Transfer tax](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/transfer-tax/?city=los-angeles) [Compare](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/compare/?a=venice&b=santa-monica)

The rules here

- **Jurisdiction:** City of Los Angeles
- **Transfer tax:** 0.45% city + 0.11% county
- **Measure ULA:** Applies Yes. 4% of the full price over $5.4M, 5.5% at $10.9M and up (2026 thresholds)
- **Rent control:** LA's Rent Stabilization Ordinance covers most apartments in buildings built before October 1, 1978
- **Public schools:** Los Angeles Unified (LAUSD)

[Run the transfer tax](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/transfer-tax/?city=los-angeles) [Compare cities](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/la-rules)

Rules have exemptions. Confirm for a specific address.

### Record king tides and big surf hit the coast on Thanksgiving morning

An extreme high tide of about 8 feet arrived Thursday morning, with a coastal flood advisory for the Malibu coast and LA County beaches through noon and a high surf warning until 9 p.m. Forecasters expect waves of roughly 6 to 11 feet with strong rip currents, and the LA Harbor tied its all-time high-water mark. If you're heading to the beach this weekend, check tide times before parking in beach lots and stay off the rocks and jetties.

What is Venice like?

Abbot Kinney Boulevard is the dinner-and-shopping strip. Ocean Front Walk, the skate park and the outdoor courts are the loud, famous part. A few blocks inland the streets go quiet, and the canals are some of the most peaceful blocks in the city.

Venice is in City of Los Angeles. City and county rules apply.

# Brentwood

Big lots, big trees, and the San Vicente coral trees.

What it’s like

The Brentwood Country Mart and San Vicente's coral tree median set the tone. Brentwood Village on Barrington is the small-town center. North of Sunset, it's estate country.

Brentwood is a City of LA neighborhood west of the 405, running from the Wilshire flats up into Mandeville Canyon. The Getty Center sits on the ridge above it.

## The pockets of Brentwood

[Every LA pocket on one map →](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/map)

In Los Angeles a single street can change the price of a house. Brentwood is really 12 smaller neighborhoods, and these are the lines between them, drawn street by street. Dashed outlines are the pockets next door.

### Brentwood Park

San Vicente Boulevard to Sunset Boulevard, 26th Street and Allenford Avenue to Cliffwood Avenue

Brentwood's estate grid, laid out around landscaped traffic circles. Big flat lots behind tall hedges, with the Brentwood Country Mart at the corner.

### Brentwood Park North of Sunset

North of Sunset Boulevard around Rockingham, Bristol and Oakmont

Estate streets climbing just above Sunset, with larger hillside lots, gated drives and canyon views over the original Brentwood Park.

### Brentwood Flats & Village

San Vicente Boulevard to Sunset Boulevard, Cliffwood Avenue to Barrington Avenue

Gently sloping streets of traditional and new-build homes between San Vicente's coral trees and Brentwood Village, the walkable cluster of shops at Sunset and Barrington.

### Brentwood Glen

Sunset Boulevard to the VA grounds, west of the 405

A tight grid of smaller-lot single-family homes tucked between the VA campus and the freeway, a short walk from Brentwood Village.

### Brentwood Terrace

San Vicente Boulevard to Montana Avenue, the Santa Monica line to Bundy Drive

Single-family streets wrapped around the Brentwood Country Club golf course, right on the Santa Monica border.

### South Brentwood

Montana Avenue to Wilshire Boulevard, the Santa Monica line to Bundy Drive

A transitional strip of single-family homes, duplexes and condos between Brentwood and Santa Monica, close to Wilshire's offices and shops.

### San Vicente Condo Corridor

San Vicente Boulevard to Wilshire Boulevard, Bundy Drive to Barrington Avenue

Brentwood's condo district: mid-rise buildings and townhomes behind San Vicente's restaurant row, the most common way into a Brentwood address.

### Mandeville Canyon

Mandeville Canyon Road and every street off it, from Sunset to the end of the canyon

A long, wooded canyon with a country feel, horse properties and big lots. Mandeville Canyon Road is one of the longest dead-end streets in the city.

### Kenter Canyon & Crestwood Hills

Kenter Avenue and the Crestwood Hills streets above it

Hillside homes in the canyon above Kenter Canyon Elementary, including Crestwood Hills, a postwar cooperative tract of modernist houses.

### Bundy Canyon

North Bundy Drive and the streets off it, up toward Mount St. Mary's

Hillside streets off Bundy Drive north of Sunset, climbing toward the Mount St. Mary's Chalon campus and the Getty ridge.

### Tigertail

Tigertail Road and its side streets north of Sunset

A narrow canyon of hillside homes off Tigertail Road, with mid-century houses and large rebuilds on view lots.

### Brentwood Heights

North of Sunset between Barrington Avenue and the 405

Hillside streets climbing from Brentwood Village toward the Getty, including gated Brentwood Circle and the Westgate Heights streets.

The story of Brentwood

## A trolley line, 87,000 trees and a boulevard of coral

Brentwood was sold in 1906 as a park you could live in. Its developers hired the man who planted Golden Gate Park, laid out winding streets around landscaped traffic circles and ran an electric railway down the middle of San Vicente Boulevard. The trains are gone, but the trees they left behind, including the coral trees that bloom red down the old tracks, are still the first thing everyone remembers about Brentwood.

4 min read 12 milestones 4 chapters 4 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1830s

The land is part of Rancho San Vicente y Santa Monica, a Mexican land grant held by the Sepulveda family.

- 1905

The Westgate tract dedicates San Vicente Boulevard, borrowing the name of the old rancho.

- 1906

The Brentwood Park tract map is recorded in January, and the tract is advertised that March as the handsomest residential park west of Chicago.

- 1900s

Pacific Electric's Westgate Line runs down the center of San Vicente, putting the tract about 25 minutes from downtown.

- 1900s

John McLaren of Golden Gate Park fame supervises the planting of some 87,000 trees and shrubs.

- 1940

The Westgate Line is shut down, leaving a wide empty median on San Vicente.

- 1948

The Brentwood Country Mart opens at 26th Street and San Vicente.

- 1950

About 120 coral trees are planted along the old trolley right-of-way.

- 1962

Marilyn Monroe buys a Spanish-style house on Fifth Helena Drive, the only home she ever owned.

- 1976

The coral trees are named City of Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument No. 148.

- 1990

A house on North Bristol Avenue becomes the TV mansion in the opening of The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air.

- 1997

The Getty Center, designed by Richard Meier, opens on the hilltop above the 405.

IBrentwood Park

### A park you could live in

**87,000** trees and shrubs planted

Brentwood started as a slice of Rancho San Vicente y Santa Monica, the old Sepulveda family grant. In 1906 the Western Pacific Development Company bought about 350 acres between the Soldiers' Home and the ocean and recorded the Brentwood Park tract. Local historians trace the name to William Lynton Brent, a major investor. The company advertised it that spring as the handsomest residential park west of Chicago.

The plan threw out the grid. Streets curved around landscaped circles and planted islands, and John McLaren, the gardener behind San Francisco's Golden Gate Park, oversaw the planting of roughly 87,000 trees and shrubs. Several of the original traffic circles still slow cars down between Sunset and San Vicente, and the canopy he planted is why Brentwood Park feels like a forest a mile from the 405.

IISan Vicente

### From trolley tracks to coral trees

**No. 148** the coral trees' monument number

To sell the lots, the developers needed a way in. An electric line ran down the middle of San Vicente Boulevard and tied into the Santa Monica line, putting Brentwood about 25 minutes from downtown Los Angeles. The line shut down in 1940, and in 1950 about 120 coral trees were planted down the empty median, their twisting gray limbs covered in red blossoms each spring.

The trees became so beloved that in 1976 the city named them Historic-Cultural Monument No. 148, and the grassy median is now a favorite running route on the Westside. Each December neighbors string them with lights.

IIIVillage life

### The Country Mart and the hilltop museum

**1948** the Country Mart opens

Brentwood's commercial life grew up along San Vicente and around the Brentwood Country Mart, a red barn-style market that opened in 1948 at 26th Street and still works like a small-town square. North of Sunset the streets climb into canyons, Mandeville, Kenter and Sullivan, where lots get bigger and the city feels far away.

In 1997 the Getty Center opened on the ridge above the 405, Richard Meier's travertine campus of galleries and gardens reached by a hillside tram. Admission is free, and on a clear day the view runs from downtown to the ocean.

IVFamous addresses

### Brentwood on screen

**1** home Marilyn Monroe ever owned

In 1962 Marilyn Monroe bought a modest Spanish-style house on Fifth Helena Drive, a cul-de-sac off Carmelina, the only house she ever owned. And the most famous Bel Air mansion on television is really in Brentwood: the house in the opening of The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air stands on North Bristol Avenue.

### Did you know?

01 **Why is there a grassy median down San Vicente?** Tap for the answer

It is where an electric railway once ran. After the tracks were removed, the median was planted with coral trees, now a city Historic-Cultural Monument.

02 **Is the Fresh Prince mansion in Bel Air?** Tap for the answer

No. The house in the opening credits is on North Bristol Avenue in Brentwood.

03 **Who planted Brentwood's trees?** Tap for the answer

John McLaren, the gardener behind Golden Gate Park, supervised the planting of about 87,000 trees and shrubs for the original tract.

04 **How much does the Getty Center cost to visit?** Tap for the answer

Admission is free. You pay only for parking, and the tram up the hill is included.

05 **What is the official tree of Los Angeles?** Tap for the answer

The coral tree, the same kind that lines the San Vicente median in Brentwood.

## Where to eat, drink and go in Brentwood

See them on the map →

Brentwood's center is San Vicente Boulevard, a coral-tree-lined median with a run of cafes and Italian restaurants, plus Barrington Court just off it. The Getty sits on the hill above, the Country Mart anchors the west end, and the trails up Mandeville Canyon start a few minutes away.

## The homes, the rules and who it fits

### The housing

Large homes and estates in Brentwood Park and north of Sunset, canyon homes in Mandeville and Kenter, and condos near San Vicente and Barrington south of Sunset.

**Good fit if**

You want space, trees and a quiet street close to the beach.

**Think twice if**

You want a bargain.

Run the numbers [Mortgage](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/mortgage) [Rent vs buy](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/rent-vs-buy) [Transfer tax](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/transfer-tax/?city=los-angeles) [Compare](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/compare/?a=brentwood&b=pacific-palisades)

The rules here

- **Jurisdiction:** City of Los Angeles
- **Transfer tax:** 0.45% city + 0.11% county
- **Measure ULA:** Applies Yes. 4% of the full price over $5.4M, 5.5% at $10.9M and up (2026 thresholds)
- **Rent control:** LA's Rent Stabilization Ordinance covers most apartments in buildings built before October 1, 1978
- **Public schools:** Los Angeles Unified (LAUSD)

[Run the transfer tax](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/transfer-tax/?city=los-angeles) [Compare cities](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/la-rules)

Rules have exemptions. Confirm for a specific address.

# Century City

High-rise living on the old 20th Century Fox backlot.

City of LA ZIP 90067 $$$ · Upper

What it’s like

Westfield Century City for shopping and dinner, wide sidewalks, and a straight shot to Beverly Hills and Westwood. A Metro D Line station is under construction on Constellation Boulevard.

Century City was built starting in the 1960s on land that was once the 20th Century Fox backlot. The studio is still next door, and the district is a City of LA neighborhood of office and condo towers.

The story of Century City

## A studio backlot that became a skyline

Century City was a movie backlot until 1961, when 20th Century Fox, short on cash, sold most of its land to Alcoa. Architects Welton Becket and Minoru Yamasaki turned the old sets into a planned city of towers, a grand hotel and a shopping center, and the Fox lot that remains still makes movies next door.

3 min read 7 milestones 3 chapters 4 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1920s

Fox Film moves production to a large lot on Pico Boulevard west of Beverly Hills.

- 1961

20th Century Fox sells most of its backlot to Alcoa, which plans a new city on it.

- 1964

The open-air shopping center, today's Westfield Century City, opens.

- 1966

The Century Plaza Hotel, designed by Minoru Yamasaki, opens.

- 1975

Yamasaki's twin triangular Century Plaza Towers are completed.

- 1987

Fox Plaza is finished.

- 1988

Fox Plaza plays Nakatomi Plaza in Die Hard.

IThe backlot

### From Western towns to office towers

**1961** Fox sells the backlot

For decades the hills between Beverly Hills and Cheviot Hills were a Fox backlot of Western towns, city streets and jungle sets. In 1961, with costs soaring, Fox sold most of the land to Alcoa, which hired Welton Becket to master-plan a city within the city: offices, apartments, a hotel and a shopping center, connected by wide boulevards including the Avenue of the Stars.

IIYamasaki

### Towers by the World Trade Center architect

**1975** Century Plaza Towers

Minoru Yamasaki, who would design New York's World Trade Center, designed the curved Century Plaza Hotel, which opened in 1966, and the twin triangular Century Plaza Towers, finished in 1975. The hotel hosted presidents and state dinners for decades and was restored and reopened in recent years.

IIIOn screen

### Nakatomi Plaza

**1988** Die Hard

The 35-story Fox Plaza, completed in 1987, became famous a year later as Nakatomi Plaza in Die Hard. The Fox studio lot right next door is still a working studio, so Century City remains one of the few places where the movie business and the office market share a fence line.

The rules here

- **Jurisdiction:** City of Los Angeles
- **Transfer tax:** 0.45% city + 0.11% county
- **Measure ULA:** Applies Yes. 4% of the full price over $5.4M, 5.5% at $10.9M and up (2026 thresholds)

- **Public schools:** Los Angeles Unified (LAUSD)

The story of Cheviot Hills & Rancho Park

## Golf courses, a saved park and Palmer's 12

Cheviot Hills grew up in the 1920s on the rolling land of an old Spanish land grant, laid out between two golf courses for the age of the automobile. Its park was saved by neighbors in the 1940s, its newer half was built on a former country club in the 1950s, and its public golf course is where Arnold Palmer famously took a 12 on a single hole.

3 min read 9 milestones 3 chapters 3 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1821

The land is part of the Spanish grant Rancho Rincon de los Bueyes.

- 1920

Hillcrest Country Club opens.

- 1921

The Rancho Golf Club opens on the land that is now Rancho Park.

- 1920s

The first Cheviot Hills tracts are laid out with curving streets, and a Pacific Electric line runs along the southern edge.

- 1945

After a neighborhood campaign, the city creates Cheviot Hills Park, about 200 acres of golf, tennis and ball fields.

- 1947

Rancho Park Golf Course is laid out in its current form.

- 1952

California Country Club Estates, known as New Cheviot, is built on a former country club.

- 1956

The Los Angeles Open moves to Rancho Park and stays through 1972.

- 1961

On January 6, Arnold Palmer takes a 12 on the course's par-5 finishing hole.

IOld and New Cheviot

### A neighborhood between fairways

**1952** New Cheviot is built

Cheviot Hills was laid out in the 1920s on rolling land between two golf clubs, with streets that curve along the contours rather than marching in a grid. Its builders hired some of the best-known residential architects of the day, including Wallace Neff, and the first house designed by Craig Ellwood stands here. In 1952 a second neighborhood, California Country Club Estates, was built on the site of a former club. Locals still call the two halves Old Cheviot and New Cheviot.

II1945

### The park the neighbors saved

**200** acres of public park and golf

The Rancho golf course changed hands several times in the 1920s and 1930s. Neighbors pushed for the city to keep it open space, and in 1945 they won: Los Angeles created Cheviot Hills Park, roughly 200 acres that include the public golf course, tennis courts, a pool and ball fields. It is one of the reasons the neighborhood feels so open.

IIIJanuary 6, 1961

### Palmer's 12

**12** strokes on one hole

Rancho Park hosted the Los Angeles Open from 1956 to 1972. On the first day of the 1961 tournament, Arnold Palmer, then the best golfer in the world, hit a fine drive on the par-5 finishing hole and then sent four straight shots out of bounds. He made a 12. A plaque at the hole marks the spot, and when asked how he managed it, Palmer reportedly said he had missed a putt for an 11.

The rules here

- **Jurisdiction:** City of Los Angeles
- **Transfer tax:** 0.45% city + 0.11% county

- **Rent control:** LA's Rent Stabilization Ordinance covers most apartments in buildings built before October 1, 1978
- **Public schools:** Los Angeles Unified (LAUSD)
