What it’s like

Downtown Culver City has the restaurants, theaters and the Metro E Line station. The Ballona Creek bike path runs to the beach. The Baldwin Hills Scenic Overlook stairs are the local workout with the best view of the basin.

Culver City is an independent city of about five square miles surrounded by Los Angeles. It's home to Sony Pictures Studios and Amazon Studios, and it runs its own schools, rent control and transfer tax.

The story of Culver City

## The Heart of Screenland

Harry Culver came west to sell real estate and figured movie studios would sell it for him. He founded his city in 1913, lured Thomas Ince and then the studio that became MGM, and for decades some of the most famous films ever made were shot on a few blocks between Washington and Culver boulevards.

3 min read 10 milestones 3 chapters 4 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1913

Harry Culver announces his new town between Los Angeles and Venice.

- 1915

Producer Thomas Ince builds a studio on Washington Boulevard.

- 1917

Culver City incorporates.

- 1918

Ince builds a second studio down the street, behind a colonial mansion facade.

- 1924

MGM is formed on the original Ince lot, and the Culver Hotel opens downtown.

- 1931

Helms Bakery opens on Venice Boulevard.

- 1932

Helms becomes the official baker of the Los Angeles Olympic Games.

- 1939

The Wizard of Oz is made at MGM, and Gone with the Wind is shot at the old Ince studio.

- 1990

Sony takes over the MGM lot, now Sony Pictures Studios.

- 2012

The Expo Line reaches Culver City.

I1913

### Harry Culver's pitch

**1917** Culver City incorporates

Harry Culver picked a spot halfway between downtown and the beach and sold it with stunts, parades and contests. His best move was recruiting the movies. Thomas Ince built a studio on Washington Boulevard in 1915 and a second one in 1918, and Culver City incorporated in 1917 with a film industry already in place.

IIThe studios

### Two lots, a hundred classics

**1939** Oz and Gone with the Wind

Ince's first lot became the home of Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer in 1924, and for decades MGM produced the musicals and epics that defined Hollywood's golden age, including The Wizard of Oz in 1939. Ince's second studio, with its white colonial mansion, became the opening logo of Selznick International, which shot Gone with the Wind there the same year. Both lots still make movies and television: the MGM lot is now Sony Pictures Studios, and the mansion lot is The Culver Studios.

IIIDowntown

### From bakery trucks to the Expo Line

**1932** Helms bakes for the Olympics

Helms Bakery opened on Venice Boulevard in 1931 and sold bread from trucks that toured LA's neighborhoods until 1969. It was the official baker of the 1932 Olympics, and its building is now a design and dining district. Downtown Culver City reinvented itself around restaurants and the Culver Hotel, built by Harry Culver in 1924, and the arrival of the Expo Line in 2012 tied it back into the regional rail network.

Test yourself

01 **What is the Culver City slogan?** Tap for the answer

The Heart of Screenland, earned by the MGM and Ince studios that made it a movie capital.

02 **Where was Gone with the Wind filmed?** Tap for the answer

At the old Thomas Ince studio on Washington Boulevard, now The Culver Studios, with its famous colonial mansion facade.

03 **Who baked the bread for the 1932 Olympics?** Tap for the answer

Helms Bakery, whose 1931 building on Venice Boulevard is now a dining and design district.

Living here

## The homes, the rules and who it fits

### The housing

1920s to 1950s houses in neighborhoods like Carlson Park and Culver Crest, hillside homes in Blair Hills, and condos in Fox Hills. Sales over $1.5M pay Culver City's bracketed transfer tax.

**Good fit if**

You want a small-city feel, walkable dinners and a train.

**Think twice if**

You're selling above $1.5M and want to avoid an extra transfer tax.

Run the numbers [Mortgage](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/mortgage) [Rent vs buy](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/rent-vs-buy) [Transfer tax](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/transfer-tax/?city=culver-city) [Compare](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/compare/?a=culver-city&b=palms)

The rules here

- **Jurisdiction:** City of Culver City
- **Transfer tax:** Measure RE brackets from 0.45% up to 4% on the top slice, plus 0.11% county
- **Measure ULA:** No No. Culver City has its own bracketed tax (Measure RE)
- **Rent control:** Culver City rent control covers most apartments built before February 1, 1995
- **Public schools:** Culver City Unified (CCUSD)

[Run the transfer tax](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/transfer-tax/?city=culver-city) [Compare cities](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/la-rules)

## Culver City: common questions

Who is a real estate agent who works in Culver City?

Nathaniel Grivas, REALTOR® (DRE #02410660) with The Brodsky Group at Compass Beverly Hills, helps people buy, sell, rent, invest and build in Culver City and across West LA, Beverly Hills and the San Fernando Valley. Call or text 310-269-5541.

What is Culver City like?

Downtown Culver City has the restaurants, theaters and the Metro E Line station. The Ballona Creek bike path runs to the beach. The Baldwin Hills Scenic Overlook stairs are the local workout with the best view of the basin.

Is Culver City its own city?

Culver City is in City of Culver City. It sets its own taxes, rules and services.

What ZIP codes cover Culver City?

Culver City is mostly ZIP 90230, 90232.

What kind of homes are in Culver City?

1920s to 1950s houses in neighborhoods like Carlson Park and Culver Crest, hillside homes in Blair Hills, and condos in Fox Hills. Sales over $1.5M pay Culver City's bracketed transfer tax.

What is the transfer tax when you sell in Culver City?

Measure RE brackets from 0.45% up to 4% on the top slice, plus 0.11% county

Does rent control apply in Culver City?

Culver City rent control covers most apartments built before February 1, 1995

Which public schools serve Culver City?

Culver City Unified (CCUSD)

Who is Culver City a good fit for?

You want a small-city feel, walkable dinners and a train.

What it’s like

Sunday means the Mar Vista Farmers Market on Grand View Boulevard. Venice Boulevard has the local restaurants and coffee. Mar Vista Hill gives you ocean views, and the rec center fills up on weekends.

Mar Vista is a City of LA neighborhood between Venice, Culver City and Palms. It grew up after World War II, and it's one of the most active new-construction areas on the Westside.

The story of Mar Vista

## Ocean Park Heights, a circus city and a modernist tract

Mar Vista started as Ocean Park Heights, a hilltop subdivision with a view of the bay, and took its Spanish name, sea view, in 1924. Next door, a circus owner briefly ran his own city. After the Second World War aircraft workers filled its streets, and architect Gregory Ain built one of the most important modernist tracts in Los Angeles.

3 min read 7 milestones 3 chapters 3 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1900s

Ocean Park Heights, an upscale subdivision on Mar Vista Hill, goes on sale. City historians call it one of LA's first gated communities.

- 1920

Al G. Barnes moves his circus winter quarters to a ranch on Washington Boulevard.

- 1924

The local chamber of commerce renames Ocean Park Heights as Mar Vista.

- 1926

Barnes City incorporates in February and votes to join Los Angeles in September.

- 1927

Mar Vista is annexed to Los Angeles.

- 1948

Gregory Ain's Mar Vista Tract of 52 modern houses is built, with landscaping by Garrett Eckbo.

- 2003

The Ain tract becomes the first historic district in the city made up entirely of postwar modern homes.

ISea view

### Ocean Park Heights becomes Mar Vista

**1924** the name Mar Vista is adopted

Before it was Mar Vista, the hill above Venice was Ocean Park Heights, a subdivision sold on its ocean views. New tracts nearby took the name Mar Vista, and so did the Red Car stop, so in 1924 the chamber of commerce made it official. Three years later the community voted to join Los Angeles.

IIBarnes City

### The circus that became a city

**7** months Barnes City lasted

In 1920 Al G. Barnes, whose traveling wild animal show was one of the biggest in the country, moved its winter quarters to a ranch on Washington Boulevard, with a zoo the public could visit. Barnes and his allies incorporated the surrounding area as Barnes City in February 1926. Neighbors who did not want to live in a city run by a circus owner pushed back, and that September the voters chose to join Los Angeles. Barnes City lasted about seven months, and the circus soon moved to the San Gabriel Valley.

III1948

### Gregory Ain's Mar Vista Tract

**52** modern houses in the Ain tract

After the war, Mar Vista filled with workers from the nearby aircraft plants. In 1948 architect Gregory Ain designed a tract of 52 small modern houses with flexible floor plans, open to their gardens, landscaped by Garrett Eckbo. In 2003 the tract became the first Historic Preservation Overlay Zone in Los Angeles made up solely of postwar modern homes, and its houses are prized by buyers who love mid-century design.

Test yourself

### Did you know?

01 **What does Mar Vista mean?** Tap for the answer

Sea view, after the views from its hill. It was called Ocean Park Heights until 1924.

02 **Did a circus really run its own city here?** Tap for the answer

Yes. Barnes City, home to the Al G. Barnes circus, incorporated in 1926 and joined Los Angeles about seven months later.

03 **What makes the Mar Vista Tract special?** Tap for the answer

It is a 1948 neighborhood of 52 modern homes by Gregory Ain, protected since 2003 as a historic district.

Living here

## The homes, the rules and who it fits

### The housing

Post-war single-family homes on lots around 5,000 to 7,000 square feet, with plenty of remodels, new builds and ADUs. The Mar Vista Tract, designed by Gregory Ain in 1948, is a protected historic district.

**Good fit if**

You want a house with a yard on the Westside and quick freeway access.

**Think twice if**

You want to walk to most of what you need.

Run the numbers [Mortgage](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/mortgage) [Rent vs buy](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/rent-vs-buy) [Transfer tax](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/transfer-tax/?city=los-angeles) [Compare](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/compare/?a=mar-vista&b=venice)

The rules here

- **Jurisdiction:** City of Los Angeles
- **Transfer tax:** 0.45% city + 0.11% county
- **Measure ULA:** Applies Yes. 4% of the full price over $5.4M, 5.5% at $10.9M and up (2026 thresholds)
- **Rent control:** LA's Rent Stabilization Ordinance covers most apartments in buildings built before October 1, 1978
- **Public schools:** Los Angeles Unified (LAUSD)

What kind of homes are in Mar Vista?

Post-war single-family homes on lots around 5,000 to 7,000 square feet, with plenty of remodels, new builds and ADUs. The Mar Vista Tract, designed by Gregory Ain in 1948, is a protected historic district.

The story of Palms

## The Westside's oldest suburb

Palms was founded in 1886 as The Palms, a farm and vacation town at a railroad stop halfway between downtown and the beach. It joined Los Angeles in 1915, the oldest neighborhood on the Westside to be annexed, and its little depot was saved, moved across town and still welcomes visitors today.

3 min read 8 milestones 2 chapters 3 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1875

A station called Bay View opens on the Los Angeles and Independence Railroad.

- 1886

The first tract map of The Palms is dated December 26, now considered the town's birthday. The founders plant thousands of trees.

- 1886-88

The Southern Pacific depot is built at the center of town.

- 1907

The Palms Chamber of Commerce forms.

- 1915

On May 22, Palms joins Los Angeles, the same day as most of the San Fernando Valley.

- 1963

The depot becomes City Historic-Cultural Monument No. 22.

- 1976

Neighbors raise money to move the depot to Heritage Square Museum.

- 2016

Rail returns as the Expo Line opens its Palms station.

I1886

### A town at a railroad stop

**1886** The Palms is founded

The Palms grew up around a train stop on the line from Los Angeles to the coast. Its founders bought land around the station, planted thousands of trees and filed their first tract map on December 26, 1886, selling lots to farmers and to city families escaping the summer heat downtown. For nearly 30 years it was a small, independent farm town.

II1915

### Joining the city, saving the depot

**No. 22** the depot's monument number

Like the Valley, Palms joined Los Angeles in 1915 for its new aqueduct water, making it the oldest neighborhood on the Westside to be annexed. The two-story wooden depot outlived the trains. Named a monument in 1963, it was moved in 1976 to Heritage Square Museum in Montecito Heights. In 2016 trains came back, when the Expo Line opened a Palms station at National and Palms boulevards.

The founders named their 1886 town The Palms and planted thousands of trees around the depot.

02 **Where is the old Palms train depot?** Tap for the answer

At Heritage Square Museum in Montecito Heights, where it was moved in 1976.

03 **When did Palms join Los Angeles?** Tap for the answer

May 22, 1915, the same day as most of the San Fernando Valley.

The story of Pico-Robertson & Beverlywood

## Two boulevards, an old rancho and Beverlywood

Pico-Robertson takes its name from the crossroads at its center: Pico Boulevard, named for Pio Pico, the last governor of Mexican California, and Robertson Boulevard. South of it, the Leimert company opened Beverlywood in 1940 with strict rules, private parks and 1,354 houses, and it still runs on them.

3 min read 4 milestones 2 chapters 2 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1840s

The land is part of a Mexican-era rancho. A later company named itself after Don Jose de Arnaz, one of its owners.

- 1931

Alexander Hamilton High School opens on Robertson Boulevard.

- 1940

The Walter H. Leimert Company opens Beverlywood with an opening-day ceremony and a homes association to enforce its rules.

- 1993

The Museum of Tolerance opens on Pico Boulevard.

IThe crossroads

### Pio Pico's boulevard

**Pio Pico** last governor of Mexican California

Pico Boulevard is named for Pio Pico, the last governor of California under Mexico,. Where it meets Robertson Boulevard grew a dense neighborhood of 1920s and 1930s duplexes, bungalows and apartment buildings, with one of the busiest walkable shopping strips on the Westside along Pico.

II1940

### Beverlywood by the rules

**1,354** houses in Beverlywood

In 1940 the Walter H. Leimert Company, which had already built Leimert Park, opened Beverlywood south of Pico-Robertson. It was planned from the start with binding covenants, conditions and restrictions and a homes association to enforce them, plus small private parks for residents. Its 1,354 single-family houses, mostly traditional styles from the 1940s, sit on curving streets that still look much as they did when the tract opened.

Test yourself

Pio Pico, the last governor of California under Mexican rule.

02 **Who built Beverlywood?** Tap for the answer

The Walter H. Leimert Company, the developer of Leimert Park, in 1940.

03 **How many houses are in Beverlywood?** Tap for the answer

1,354 single-family homes, governed by a homes association founded in 1940.

The rules here

- **Jurisdiction:** City of Los Angeles
- **Transfer tax:** 0.45% city + 0.11% county
- **Measure ULA:** Applies Yes. 4% of the full price over $5.4M, 5.5% at $10.9M and up (2026 thresholds)
- **Rent control:** LA's Rent Stabilization Ordinance covers most apartments in buildings built before October 1, 1978
- **Public schools:** Los Angeles Unified (LAUSD)

The story of West LA & Sawtelle

## The Soldiers' City and Sawtelle Japantown

West LA grew up around an old soldiers' home. When the federal government opened a branch of the National Home for Disabled Volunteer Soldiers here in 1888, a town called Sawtelle grew up around it, incorporated as its own city and held out until Los Angeles absorbed it in 1922. By then nurseries lined Sawtelle Boulevard, and in 2015 the city named the district Sawtelle Japantown.

3 min read 9 milestones 2 chapters 3 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1888

The Pacific Branch of the National Home for Disabled Volunteer Soldiers opens.

- 1899

The City of Sawtelle incorporates, named for W.E. Sawtelle of the Pacific Land Company.

- 1906

The Soldiers' Home becomes a stop on a popular trolley sightseeing tour.

- 1910s

Japanese immigrant farmers settle in the area, then still mostly fields.

- 1918

In the middle of a court fight over annexation, Los Angeles police raid Sawtelle's city hall and carry off its records.

- 1922

Sawtelle is consolidated into the City of Los Angeles.

- 1941

There are 26 Japanese American nurseries along and near Sawtelle Boulevard.

- 1942

Japanese American families here are forcibly removed and incarcerated. Many return after the war and rebuild.

- 2015

The city designates Sawtelle Japantown.

I1888

### The Soldiers' City

**1888** the Soldiers' Home opens

The Pacific Branch of the National Home for Disabled Volunteer Soldiers opened in 1888 to care for Civil War veterans, and the town of Sawtelle grew around its gates. Incorporated in 1899, Sawtelle was independent for more than 20 years. Los Angeles wanted it, and the fight got ugly: in 1918, with the case still in court, LAPD officers raided Sawtelle City Hall and seized its records. The consolidation was finished in 1922. The soldiers' home lives on as the West Los Angeles VA campus.

IINurseries

### The gardeners of Sawtelle

**26** nurseries by 1941

Japanese immigrants began farming here in the 1910s, and by the 1930s Sawtelle Boulevard was lined with nurseries and garden supply shops serving the Westside's new estates and the gardeners who tended them. In 1942 those families were forcibly removed and incarcerated under wartime orders. Many came back and rebuilt. A few legacy nurseries still operate, and the restaurants and shops along the boulevard carry the story forward. The city recognized the district as Sawtelle Japantown in 2015.

Apartments and townhome-style condos, with smaller single-family homes south of Olympic. Good condo inventory for first-time buyers.

The rules here

- **Jurisdiction:** City of Los Angeles
- **Transfer tax:** 0.45% city + 0.11% county
- **Measure ULA:** Applies Yes. 4% of the full price over $5.4M, 5.5% at $10.9M and up (2026 thresholds)
- **Rent control:** LA's Rent Stabilization Ordinance covers most apartments in buildings built before October 1, 1978
- **Public schools:** Los Angeles Unified (LAUSD)

Post-war houses, real yards, and LMU on the bluff.

What it’s like

Suburban and steady: Kentwood and Westport Heights for houses, the Sepulveda and Manchester corridors for errands, Westchester Park for sports. The closer you get to LAX, the more you hear the planes.

Westchester grew up in the 1940s around LAX and the aircraft plants. It's a City of LA neighborhood with Loyola Marymount University on the bluff above Playa Vista.

## The pockets of Westchester

[Every LA pocket on one map →](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/map)

In Los Angeles a single street can change the price of a house. Westchester is really 4 smaller neighborhoods, and these are the lines between them, drawn street by street. Dashed outlines are the pockets next door.

### Kentwood

Manchester Avenue north to the bluffs, Loyola Boulevard to Sepulveda

Kentwood: a 1940s and 1950s tract of single-family homes near Loyola Marymount, with ocean-close weather.

### Loyola Village

Manchester Avenue to Westchester Parkway, Lincoln to Sepulveda

Loyola Village: post-war single-family streets south of Manchester near Westchester Park.

### Westport Heights

Manchester Avenue north to the bluffs, Sepulveda to Airport Boulevard

Westport Heights: single-family streets on the bluffs east of Sepulveda with views toward the city.

### Osage & East Westchester

Manchester Avenue south, Sepulveda to Aviation

Westchester east of Sepulveda: single-family streets and apartments between the town center and the airport.

The story of Westchester

## LAX, Loyola and a suburb built for aircraft workers

Westchester was bean fields until 1928, when the city took over a small airfield called Mines Field and the Jesuits broke ground for a new Loyola campus on the bluffs. When the aircraft plants boomed in the 1940s, builders like Fritz Burns put up thousands of small houses for their workers, and the neighborhood grew up around the airport that became LAX.

3 min read 9 milestones 3 chapters 3 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1928

Los Angeles leases 640 acres for an airport at Mines Field, named for the broker who arranged the deal.

- 1928

Loyola breaks ground on the bluffs, with developer Fritz Burns riding around the ceremony on horseback.

- 1929

Loyola opens its new campus on the bluffs, and the Graf Zeppelin moors at Mines Field on its flight around the world.

- 1932

Westchester hosts the cross-country leg of the Olympic equestrian event.

- 1941

The first big tract of homes opens on December 6, the day before Pearl Harbor.

- 1940s

Fritz Burns and other builders raise thousands of small houses for workers at the nearby aircraft plants.

- 1949

The airport is renamed Los Angeles International Airport.

- 1961

The Theme Building opens at the center of LAX.

- 1973

Loyola and Marymount merge as Loyola Marymount University.

I1928

### An airfield in the bean fields

**640** acres leased for the airport in 1928

In 1928 the city leased 640 acres of farmland for a municipal airport at Mines Field, and the following year the German airship Graf Zeppelin tied up there on its trip around the world. The same year Loyola College moved its campus to the bluffs above the Ballona wetlands on land donated with help from Harry Culver. The college became Loyola Marymount University in 1973.

IIThe 1940s

### Burns homes

**1941** the first big tract opens

When the aircraft industry exploded during the Second World War, its workers needed somewhere to live. Developer Fritz Burns, who had been selling lots here since the 1920s, built neighborhoods of modest two- and three-bedroom houses for them, and much of Westchester's housing still dates from those years. Many buyers today are drawn to those same single-story houses, on lots big enough to expand.

III1961

### The Theme Building

**1961** the Theme Building opens

As the airport became LAX, the city commissioned a landmark for its center. The Theme Building, with its arches straddling a flying saucer of a restaurant, opened in 1961, designed by a team including Paul R. Williams. Airport growth also took its toll: over the decades Westchester lost thousands of homes to expansion and noise buyouts.

Test yourself

### Did you know?

01 **Why was the airport called Mines Field?** Tap for the answer

After William Mines, the real estate broker who arranged the 1928 lease.

02 **Did the Graf Zeppelin really land here?** Tap for the answer

Yes. It moored at Mines Field in 1929 during its flight around the world.

03 **Who designed the LAX Theme Building?** Tap for the answer

A team of architects that included Paul R. Williams. It opened in 1961.

Living here

## The homes, the rules and who it fits

### The housing

1940s and 1950s single-family homes on lots around 5,000 to 7,000 square feet, with a lot of remodels and new builds. One of the better values for a Westside house with a yard.

**Good fit if**

You want a house and a yard on the Westside for less, and you fly a lot.

**Think twice if**

Plane noise bothers you.

The rules here

- **Jurisdiction:** City of Los Angeles
- **Transfer tax:** 0.45% city + 0.11% county
- **Measure ULA:** Applies Yes. 4% of the full price over $5.4M, 5.5% at $10.9M and up (2026 thresholds)
- **Rent control:** LA's Rent Stabilization Ordinance covers most apartments in buildings built before October 1, 1978
- **Public schools:** Los Angeles Unified (LAUSD)

# Westwood

UCLA, Westwood Village and the Wilshire Corridor towers.

City of LA ZIP 90024 $$$$ · Top of market

Get Westwood listings What's my Westwood home worth?

What it’s like

Westwood Village has the old movie palaces, the Hammer Museum and campus energy. The Wilshire Corridor is condo living with doormen. North of Wilshire, the residential streets are quiet and tree-lined. The Metro D Line subway extension to Westwood is under construction.

Westwood is the City of LA neighborhood around UCLA, from the Wilshire Corridor high-rises to the single-family streets of Westwood Hills and Holmby Westwood.

[Walkable](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/#walkable) [Condo friendly](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/#condo) [Residential streets](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/#family) [Near Metro rail](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/#transit)

Block by block

## The pockets of Westwood

[Every LA pocket on one map →](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/map)

In Los Angeles a single street can change the price of a house. Westwood is really 6 smaller neighborhoods, and these are the lines between them, drawn street by street. Dashed outlines are the pockets next door.

### Westwood Village

Wilshire Boulevard to Le Conte Avenue, Gayley Avenue to Hilgard Avenue

Westwood Village: the shopping and dining district at UCLA's front door, with apartments and condos.

### North Village

Wilshire Boulevard to Sunset, Veteran Avenue to Gayley Avenue

North Westwood: apartments and condos west of campus, plus single-family streets near Veteran Avenue.

### Little Holmby

Wilshire Boulevard to Sunset, Hilgard Avenue to Beverly Glen Boulevard

Little Holmby: a small grid of large homes between campus and Holmby Hills, among the most sought after streets in Westwood.

### Holmby Westwood

Wilshire Boulevard to Santa Monica Boulevard, Westwood Boulevard to Beverly Glen

Holmby-Westwood: single-family streets south of Wilshire's condo corridor, close to the Village and Century City.

### Westwood South of Wilshire

Wilshire Boulevard to Santa Monica Boulevard, Sepulveda Boulevard to Westwood Boulevard

The blocks south of the Village: a mix of apartments, condos and some single-family homes near the Westwood Library.

### Westwood South of Santa Monica

Santa Monica Boulevard to Pico, Sepulveda Boulevard to Beverly Glen

Westwood south of Santa Monica Boulevard: single-family streets around Westwood Park and the Westside Pavilion, plus apartments near the boulevards.

The story of Westwood

## A village built around a university

In the early 1920s the Janss family set out to develop the old Wolfskill ranch west of Beverly Hills with a plan: help bring the University of California to its hills, then sell everyone else the homes and shops around it. UCLA moved in in 1929, Westwood Village opened the same year, and its Spanish-style streets and movie palaces became the Westside's downtown.

3 min read 8 milestones 3 chapters 4 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1919

Department store owner Arthur Letts buys the old Wolfskill ranch, and the Janss Investment Company takes on its development.

- 1919

The Southern Branch of the University of California opens on Vermont Avenue in East Hollywood.

- 1922

The first Westwood residential tracts go on sale.

- 1925

Voters in Los Angeles and nearby cities approve bonds to buy the Westwood campus site.

- 1929

On May 31, UCLA moves to Westwood behind a police motorcade. Westwood Village opens the same year.

- 1931

The Fox Village Theatre opens with its landmark tower.

- 1937

The Bruin Theatre opens across the street.

- 1990

The Hammer Museum opens on Wilshire.

IThe Janss plan

### Selling a college town

**1929** UCLA and the Village open

The Janss brothers took over thousands of acres of ranch land between Beverly Hills and Sawtelle and made the University of California the centerpiece of their plan. With a campus on the hill, they reasoned, the houses and shops around it would sell themselves. Voters approved bonds to buy the campus land in 1925, and the Janss company laid out Westwood Village below it, with Mediterranean architecture, tile roofs and design rules for every building.

IIMay 31, 1929

### UCLA moves west

**Chemistry 1A** the first class taught in Westwood

UCLA began on Vermont Avenue in East Hollywood in 1919 and outgrew it within a decade. On May 31, 1929, classes on Vermont were dismissed early and a police motorcade led trucks of furniture to the new campus, where Royce Hall and the library stood almost alone on the hill. The first class held in Westwood was Chemistry 1A.

IIIPremiere night

### The Village and its theaters

**1931** the Fox Village Theatre opens

Westwood Village opened alongside the university and quickly became the Westside's shopping district. The Fox Village Theatre, with its white tower, opened in 1931, and the Bruin followed in 1937. The two theaters still host Hollywood premieres, and the Village remains one of the few walkable, master-planned business districts of its era in Los Angeles.

The story of Bel Air

## An oilman's private park in the hills

Bel Air was planned before it was built. Oilman Alphonzo Bell bought a ranch in the Santa Monica Mountains, buried the power lines, set minimums on what buyers had to spend, put gates at the entrances and opened it in 1923 as a residential park. A century, a country club, a famous hotel and one devastating fire later, it is still laid out almost exactly as he drew it.

3 min read 9 milestones 4 chapters 4 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1922

Alphonzo Bell, whose fortune came from oil found on his family's Santa Fe Springs farm, runs water, sewer and underground power and phone lines into his hillside ranch.

- 1923

The first Bel Air tract opens: 128 lots on Bel Air Road and the streets off it, behind the East Gate at Sunset and Beverly Glen.

- 1925

A second tract expands the community, and the Bel-Air Country Club opens. Its golf course follows in 1927.

- 1931

Bell starts adding the land that becomes the rest of Bel Air, up the canyons toward Mulholland.

- 1933

The Kirkeby Mansion, later the Beverly Hillbillies house, is built on Bel Air Road.

- 1942

The Bel Air Association forms to protect the look of the community. It still meets at the East Gate.

- 1946

Texas hotelier Joseph Drown buys Bell's old sales office and 18 acres in Stone Canyon and opens the Hotel Bel-Air.

- 1961

On November 6, the Bel Air Fire, driven by Santa Ana winds, destroys 484 homes.

- 1989

Ronald and Nancy Reagan retire to a house on St. Cloud Road.

IThe founder

### Alphonzo Bell's master plan

**128** lots in the original 1923 tract

Alphonzo Bell made his money when oil was struck on his family's farm in Santa Fe Springs, and he spent it on a ranch in the hills west of Beverly Hills. Before selling a single lot he graded roads, piped in water and sewers, and put electric and telephone lines underground, which was almost unheard of in 1922. Deed restrictions required buyers to spend a set minimum building their homes.

The first tract opened in 1923 with 128 lots along Bel Air Road and the streets that branch from it, entered through the East Gate at Sunset Boulevard and Beverly Glen. That original allotment is what people still call Old Bel Air or East Gate. Bell kept adding land through the 1930s, and the community grew up the canyons toward Mulholland.

IIThe clubs

### A country club and a hotel in a canyon

**1946** the Hotel Bel-Air opens

Bell built the Bel-Air Country Club into the plan from the start. The club opened in 1925 and its golf course, threaded through the canyons and across a famous swinging bridge, followed in 1927.

In 1946 a Texas hotel man named Joseph Drown bought 18 acres in Stone Canyon, including the Mission-style buildings Bell had used as his planning and sales office, and turned them into the Hotel Bel-Air. With its swan pond, gardens and bungalows, it became Hollywood's favorite hideaway, and it remains the community's living room.

IIIFire

### November 6, 1961

**484** homes lost in the 1961 fire

On November 6, 1961, a brush fire in the Santa Monica Mountains, pushed by Santa Ana winds, jumped the ridge and swept down the canyons of Bel Air and Brentwood. In two days it destroyed 484 homes, including houses owned by well-known film stars, and injured about 200 firefighters.

The rebuilding that followed reshaped the hills, and the disaster changed how Los Angeles thinks about building in brush country, from clearing vegetation around homes to safer roofing. Those lessons are part of every hillside purchase here today.

IVBel Air on screen

### Famous addresses, and a famous mix-up

**1933** the Beverly Hillbillies mansion is built

The mansion Jed Clampett moved into on The Beverly Hillbillies was really the Kirkeby estate on Bel Air Road, built in 1933. Ronald and Nancy Reagan retired to St. Cloud Road in 1989.

The most famous Bel Air house on television is not in Bel Air at all. The mansion in the opening of The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air sits on Bristol Avenue in Brentwood.

The Kirkeby estate on Bel Air Road, built in 1933.

## The homes, the rules and who it fits

### The housing

Estates, hillside view homes and new spec mansions. Hillside building rules cap size, and because most sales here clear $5.4M, Measure ULA hits a large share of them.

**Good fit if**

You want maximum privacy and land close to the Westside.

**Think twice if**

You want a neighborhood you can walk.

The rules here

- **Jurisdiction:** City of Los Angeles
- **Transfer tax:** 0.45% city + 0.11% county
- **Measure ULA:** Applies Yes. 4% of the full price over $5.4M, 5.5% at $10.9M and up (2026 thresholds)
- **Rent control:** LA's Rent Stabilization Ordinance covers most apartments in buildings built before October 1, 1978
- **Public schools:** Los Angeles Unified (LAUSD)

# Beverly Hills

What it’s like

Rodeo Drive and the Golden Triangle for shopping, Beverly Gardens Park along Santa Monica Boulevard, and the Flats: gridded streets of big homes between Santa Monica Boulevard and Sunset. Trousdale Estates in the hills is mid-century modern territory.

Beverly Hills is an independent city of about 5.7 square miles surrounded by Los Angeles. It has its own police and fire departments and its own school district.

Block by block

## The pockets of Beverly Hills

[Every LA pocket on one map →](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/map)

In Los Angeles a single street can change the price of a house. Beverly Hills is really 6 smaller neighborhoods, and these are the lines between them, drawn street by street. Dashed outlines are the pockets next door.

### Beverly Hills Flats

Santa Monica Boulevard north to Sunset Boulevard, Doheny Drive west to the city line

The classic Beverly Hills flats: wide palm and jacaranda streets of large homes on big lots, a short walk to the Golden Triangle and Beverly Gardens Park.

### Golden Triangle

Wilshire Boulevard, Santa Monica Boulevard and Canon Drive

The Golden Triangle: Rodeo Drive, Canon Drive and the city's retail and office core, with a small number of condos and apartments.

### East Beverly Hills

South of Santa Monica Boulevard to Wilshire, east of Canon Drive to the city line

Smaller lots than the flats north of Santa Monica Boulevard, mixing single-family homes, duplexes and low-rise apartments a few blocks from the Golden Triangle.

### Beverly Hills South of Wilshire

South of Wilshire Boulevard to the city line

South Beverly Hills: tree-lined grids of single-family homes, duplexes and apartments around Roxbury Park and La Cienega Park, served by the Beverly Hills schools.

### Trousdale Estates

The hillside streets around Loma Vista Drive and Trousdale Place above Sunset

Trousdale Estates: mid-century view homes on flat pads cut into the hills, with gated drives and city-to-ocean views.

### Beverly Hills North of Sunset

Hillside streets north of Sunset inside the city line, around Lexington Road and Benedict Canyon's mouth

The Beverly Hills side of the canyons north of Sunset: large estates on winding streets, still inside city limits and city services.

The story of Beverly Hills

## The town that struck water instead of oil

Beverly Hills began as a failed oil play. The investors who drilled the old Rancho Rodeo de las Aguas found water instead, so they built a town around it, a hotel to sell it, and curving streets each lined with its own kind of tree. Then the movie stars arrived, voted to stay independent, and turned about 5.7 square miles into the most famous ZIP code in the world.

4 min read 14 milestones 4 chapters 6 landmarks

### Timeline

- Rancho era

The land is Rancho Rodeo de las Aguas, the gathering of the waters, where streams from Benedict, Coldwater and Franklin canyons meet.

- 1900

Oilmen Burton Green, Charles Canfield, Max Whittier and partners buy the rancho and drill. They mostly find water.

- 1906

The group reorganizes as the Rodeo Land and Water Company and names the town after Beverly Farms, Massachusetts.

- 1907

The first house goes up on a plan by landscape architect Wilbur Cook: curving streets above Santa Monica Boulevard.

- 1912

The Beverly Hills Hotel opens on the spot where the waters met, built to bring in buyers.

- 1914

Beverly Hills incorporates on January 28 with about 550 residents.

- 1919

Mary Pickford and Douglas Fairbanks buy on Summit Drive and create Pickfair. The movie colony follows.

- 1923

On April 24, voters reject annexation to Los Angeles after eight film stars campaign door to door.

- 1926

Will Rogers is named the city's honorary mayor.

- 1928

Greystone, the Doheny family's 55-room mansion by Gordon Kaufmann, is completed above Sunset.

- 1949

Paul R. Williams adds the Crescent Wing and the script logo to the newly pink Beverly Hills Hotel.

- 1954

Builder Paul Trousdale buys about 410 acres of the Doheny Ranch. It becomes Trousdale Estates.

- 1965

The city buys Greystone to save it from demolition. It opens as a public park in 1971.

- 1990

Two Rodeo, a cobbled shopping street at Wilshire and Rodeo, opens.

IThe gathering of the waters

### An oil company that found a town

**550** residents when the city incorporated in 1914

Before it had a name, this was Rancho Rodeo de las Aguas, the gathering of the waters, where streams draining Benedict, Coldwater and Franklin canyons met near today's Sunset Boulevard and Beverly Drive. In 1900 a group of oilmen including Burton Green bought the land, drilled, and came up mostly with water. In 1906 they reorganized as the Rodeo Land and Water Company, named the place after Beverly Farms, Massachusetts, and started selling lots instead of oil.

Green hired landscape architect Wilbur Cook to make it a garden city: curving streets north of Santa Monica Boulevard, a long park along the boulevard, and different street trees on different streets so blocks have their own canopy. To bring in buyers, the company built the Beverly Hills Hotel in 1912 on the spot where the waters met. It worked. By 1914 there were enough residents to incorporate, about 550 of them.

IIThe movie colony

### The stars who kept Beverly Hills independent

**8** film stars who campaigned against annexation

In 1919 Mary Pickford and Douglas Fairbanks, then the most famous couple in the world, bought a hunting lodge on Summit Drive and had it remade into Pickfair. Other stars followed them up the hill, and Beverly Hills became the place Hollywood went home to at night.

By 1923 the town was running short of water, and joining Los Angeles looked like the fix. Pickford, Fairbanks, Will Rogers, Rudolph Valentino, Harold Lloyd, Tom Mix, Conrad Nagel and Fred Niblo campaigned against it door to door. Supporters of annexation answered by leaving bottles of the local sulfur-smelling water on doorsteps. On April 24, 1923, voters chose independence anyway. Rogers was named honorary mayor in 1926, and the eight stars are honored today by the Celluloid Monument.

IIIGreystone and Trousdale

### The Doheny land above Sunset

**410** acres of Doheny Ranch that became Trousdale

Oilman Edward L. Doheny owned the hills above the flats. In 1928 the family completed Greystone, a Tudor Revival mansion of about 46,000 square feet designed by Gordon Kaufmann as a gift for his son. When a later owner planned to tear it down, the city bought the estate in 1965, and in 1971 its gardens opened as a public park. It is still one of the most filmed houses in Los Angeles.

In 1954 builder Paul Trousdale bought about 410 acres of the Doheny Ranch, persuaded Beverly Hills to bring it into the city, and laid out roughly 530 terraced lots with an architectural committee approving every house. Architects including Paul R. Williams, Wallace Neff and A. Quincy Jones designed low, glassy homes oriented to the views, and Trousdale became the mid-century address of Elvis Presley, Frank Sinatra, Dean Martin, Ray Charles and Richard Nixon. City rules still limit building height on most lots to protect those views.

IVRodeo and the Pink Palace

### From a farm town to the Golden Triangle

**1949** the year the hotel got its script logo

South of Santa Monica Boulevard, Cook's grid became the business district now called the Golden Triangle. Rodeo Drive took its modern shape in the 1960s and 1970s as designer boutiques replaced neighborhood shops, and Two Rodeo, a cobbled European-style lane at Wilshire, opened in 1990.

The Beverly Hills Hotel was painted pink in 1948, and the next year architect Paul R. Williams added the Crescent Wing and drew the script logo that is still on the sign. He also reshaped the Polo Lounge and the Fountain Coffee Room. More than a century after it opened, the hotel is still the social center the founders built it to be.

01 **Why is it called Beverly Hills?** Tap for the answer

Burton Green named it after Beverly Farms, Massachusetts, a seaside town he remembered fondly. The Hills part described the land.

02 **How did the town get started?** Tap for the answer

Oil investors drilled the old rancho in 1900 and found water instead, so they sold homes rather than oil.

03 **How close did Beverly Hills come to joining LA?** Tap for the answer

In 1923 voters were asked to annex to Los Angeles for its water. A campaign led by eight movie stars helped defeat it on April 24, 1923.

04 **Why do so many streets look different from each other?** Tap for the answer

Planner Wilbur Cook gave different streets different trees, so many blocks have their own signature canopy.

05 **Who drew the Beverly Hills Hotel's famous script logo?** Tap for the answer

What it’s like

Coldwater Canyon, Benedict Canyon and Franklin Canyon, with Mulholland on top. Franklin Canyon Park has a lake and trails, and TreePeople's park sits at Coldwater and Mulholland.

Beverly Hills Post Office, or BHPO, is the hillside area above Beverly Hills that uses the 90210 ZIP code but sits in the City of Los Angeles. That means LA's transfer tax, Measure ULA and LAUSD schools apply here.

The story of Beverly Hills Post Office

## The 90210 that's really Los Angeles

The hills north of Beverly Hills never joined the city below them. In the 1920s the federal government simply had the Beverly Hills post office deliver their mail, and three canyons got the most famous ZIP code in America by accident. Behind that address are the streams that created Beverly Hills in the first place, a reservoir built for the aqueduct, and a lake every TV fan has seen.

3 min read 10 milestones 4 chapters 3 landmarks

### Timeline

- Rancho era

Benedict, Coldwater and Franklin canyons carry the streams that meet below as the gathering of the waters.

- 1888

Trout are still being caught in Coldwater Creek.

- 1914

Beverly Hills incorporates without the hills to its north, which stay rural, much of them Doheny Ranch.

- 1914

William Mulholland and the city water department start a reservoir in upper Franklin Canyon to store new aqueduct water.

- 1920s

Washington assigns the canyons to the Beverly Hills post office. The BHPO name sticks.

- 1923

Developer George Read buys 80 acres east of Coldwater Canyon and lays out the Crests.

- 1925

Rudolph Valentino buys a Benedict Canyon estate and names it Falcon Lair.

- 1934

Franklin Canyon plays the country road in the hitchhiking scene of It Happened One Night.

- 1960

Andy Griffith and Ron Howard walk to the fishing hole at Franklin Lake for the show's opening.

- 1978

Proposition 13 closes the property tax gap between LA and Beverly Hills.

IAn address, not a city

### How the hills got 90210

**90210** a Beverly Hills ZIP in the City of LA

When Beverly Hills incorporated in 1914, the steep land to the north was left out. It stayed rural for years, much of it part of the Doheny Ranch, and in the 1920s the federal government decided the nearest post office, in Beverly Hills, would deliver its mail. That is the whole origin of BHPO. Homes here carry a Beverly Hills mailing address and the 90210 ZIP code, but they sit in the City of Los Angeles, with LA's police, fire department, schools and building rules.

For decades that came with higher property taxes than the city next door. Proposition 13 in 1978 evened that out, and the canyons became one of the most direct ways to own a 90210 address on a larger, more private lot.

IIThree canyons

### Benedict, Coldwater and Franklin

**3** canyons that fed the gathering of the waters

Each canyon has its own character. Benedict Canyon winds north from the Beverly Hills Hotel and held some of early Hollywood's grandest hideaways, including Falcon Lair, the Spanish-style estate Rudolph Valentino bought in 1925 and named after a film he never made. Coldwater Canyon is the main pass over the mountains to Studio City. Trout were still caught in its creek in the 1880s, and the park at its top is now home to TreePeople, the nonprofit that has planted trees across Los Angeles for decades.

The Doheny family used Franklin Canyon as a summer retreat, and in 1914 the city built a reservoir in it to store water from the new Owens Valley aqueduct. Today it is a park with a lake, a duck pond and miles of trails, a slice of countryside hidden in the middle of the city.

IIIOn screen

### The most filmed lake you've never visited

**1960** Andy and Opie's walk to the fishing hole

Because it looks like the countryside but sits minutes from the studios, Franklin Canyon has been a filming location since the 1930s. The hitchhiking scene in It Happened One Night was shot here, and in 1960 Andy Griffith and Ron Howard walked its shoreline with fishing poles for the opening of The Andy Griffith Show, where the reservoir played Myers Lake. Bonanza, Lassie, Star Trek and many more productions followed.

IVBeverly Crest

### The Crests and the ridge

**80** acres George Read bought in 1923

In 1923 developer George Read bought 80 acres east of Coldwater Canyon and laid out the Crests, the streets like Readcrest and Lindacrest that gave Beverly Crest its name. The area now climbs to Mulholland Drive, where the lots get bigger and the views take in both the basin and the San Fernando Valley.

Test yourself

### Did you know?

01 **Is BHPO part of Beverly Hills?** Tap for the answer

No. It is in the City of Los Angeles. The name comes from the post office that delivers its mail, which is why homes here have the 90210 ZIP code.

02 **Where is Mayberry's fishing hole?** Tap for the answer

Franklin Lake in Franklin Canyon Park, a reservoir started in 1914. It played Myers Lake in the opening of The Andy Griffith Show.

03 **Why do these canyons matter to Beverly Hills?** Tap for the answer

Their streams met below at the gathering of the waters, which gave the old rancho its name and the young town its water.

04 **Who lived at Falcon Lair?** Tap for the answer

Rudolph Valentino bought it in 1925 and named it after his unmade film The Hooded Falcon. The original house was later torn down.

## The homes, the rules and who it fits

### The housing

Hillside homes and view lots. LA's Baseline Hillside Ordinance limits how big you can build, and most of the area is in a high fire hazard zone, which affects insurance.

**Good fit if**

You want privacy and views 10 minutes from Beverly Hills.

**Think twice if**

You want to walk anywhere, or you assumed 90210 means Beverly Hills schools.

Run the numbers [Mortgage](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/mortgage) [Rent vs buy](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/rent-vs-buy) [Transfer tax](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/transfer-tax/?city=los-angeles) [Compare](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/compare/?a=bhpo&b=beverly-hills)

The rules here

- **Jurisdiction:** City of Los Angeles
- **Transfer tax:** 0.45% city + 0.11% county
- **Measure ULA:** Applies Yes. 4% of the full price over $5.4M, 5.5% at $10.9M and up (2026 thresholds)
- **Rent control:** LA's Rent Stabilization Ordinance covers most apartments in buildings built before October 1, 1978
- **Public schools:** Los Angeles Unified (LAUSD)

The story of Hollywood Hills

## A billboard, a secret studio and a canyon full of songs

The Hollywood Hills were sold to Los Angeles one gimmick at a time: an electric trolley up a dirt canyon, an inn on a summit, and a giant billboard that was supposed to come down after a year and a half. A century later the billboard is the most famous sign on earth, the canyon wrote the soundtrack of the 1960s, and the ridge road named for the city's water chief is still the best drive in town.

5 min read 12 milestones 4 chapters 7 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1908

Lookout Mountain Park and Water Co. buys 280 acres above Laurel Canyon and starts selling Bungalow Land vacation lots.

- 1910

A trackless electric trolley, one of the first trolley bus lines in the country, starts hauling buyers up Laurel Canyon for a dime.

- 1918

Fire destroys the Lookout Mountain Inn on the summit, and the trolley stops running the same year.

- 1922

The Hollywood Bowl holds its first season in a natural amphitheater off Cahuenga Pass.

- 1923

The HOLLYWOODLAND sign goes up on Mount Lee to sell lots in Beachwood Canyon: 13 letters, about 4,000 bulbs, $21,000.

- 1924

Mulholland Drive opens along the ridge, and developer Cooley Butler lays out the first Bird Streets above the Sunset Strip.

- 1947

The Air Force quietly opens Lookout Mountain Air Force Station, a classified film studio on Wonderland Avenue.

- 1949

The Hollywood Chamber of Commerce takes over the sign, drops LAND, and it becomes simply HOLLYWOOD.

- 1960

John Lautner's Chemosphere and Pierre Koenig's Stahl House are finished, and Blue Jay Way joins the Bird Streets.

- 1967

George Harrison writes Blue Jay Way at a rented house on the street while waiting out the fog.

- 1969

The secret studio closes after producing more than 6,500 films, and it later becomes a private home.

- 1978

The crumbling sign is rebuilt in steel, paid for by nine donors at $27,700 a letter.

IBeachwood Canyon

### The sign was an ad

**45 ft** height of each letter

In 1923 a syndicate that included Los Angeles Times publisher Harry Chandler opened Hollywoodland, a hillside tract at the top of Beachwood Canyon. To get it noticed they built a billboard on Mount Lee: thirteen sheet-metal letters about 45 feet tall, wired with roughly 4,000 bulbs that flashed HOLLY, then WOOD, then LAND, then the whole word. It cost about $21,000 and was meant to last about 18 months.

The tract still looks the way it was sold, with stone gateway towers on Beachwood Drive and hand-built stone walls and public staircases climbing between the streets. The sign outlived the sales campaign. By 1949 the city owned the land, the Chamber of Commerce agreed to repair the first nine letters, and LAND came down. In 1978 the original was too far gone to save, so it was rebuilt in steel, one sponsored letter at a time.

IILaurel Canyon

### From Bungalow Land to the music canyon

**6,500+** classified films made on Wonderland Avenue

Laurel Canyon started as a weekend escape. Around 1908 developers carved out Bungalow Land and Wonderland Park, small lots on narrow lanes, and ran a trackless electric trolley up the dirt road from Sunset so buyers could see them. A roadhouse at Lookout Mountain Avenue served lunch, and an inn on the summit looked out over the whole basin until fire took it in 1918.

After the Second World War the Air Force hid a film studio on Wonderland Avenue, where crews processed and edited classified footage of nuclear tests from 1947 to 1969. Most neighbors never knew. In the same years the canyon below filled with musicians: Joni Mitchell, Cass Elliot of the Mamas and the Papas, David Crosby, Jim Morrison and Frank Zappa, whose log cabin at Laurel Canyon and Lookout Mountain hosted endless jam sessions until it burned in 1981. The Canyon Country Store, the general store at the center of it all, is still open.

IIIAbove the Strip

### The Bird Streets

**1924** the first Bird Streets laid out

The Bird Streets began in 1924, when developer Cooley Butler laid out roads on the ridge just above the Sunset Strip, and they kept growing for four decades: Oriole, Thrasher, Nightingale, Warbler and the rest of the flock. Blue Jay Way arrived in 1960 and Skylark Lane in 1964. As recently as 2017, a street here was renamed Hummingbird Place to join them.

In August 1967 George Harrison rented a house on Blue Jay Way and wrote the song of the same name on an organ there, waiting for a friend who was lost in the fog on the winding streets. Today the flat pads cut into the hillside and the open views from downtown to the ocean make these some of the most sought-after streets in the Hills.

IVThe ridge

### Mulholland and the houses that float

**1913** the aqueduct Mulholland built

Mulholland Drive opened in 1924 along the spine of the Santa Monica Mountains, named for William Mulholland, the self-taught engineer whose aqueduct brought Owens Valley water to the city in 1913. The road runs about 21 miles, with a stretch through the western hills still unpaved, and every turnout gives you the city on one side and the Valley on the other.

The steep lots that made the Hills hard to build on made them perfect for architects with something to prove. In 1960 John Lautner balanced the Chemosphere, an eight-sided house, on a single concrete column above a slope most builders had written off. The same year Pierre Koenig finished the Stahl House, Case Study House No. 22, and Julius Shulman photographed its glass corner floating over the lights of the city. Both are landmarks now, and both still define what a house in the Hills can be.

Test yourself

### Did you know?

01 **Why does the sign only say HOLLYWOOD?** Tap for the answer

It went up in 1923 as HOLLYWOODLAND, an ad for a housing tract. When the Chamber of Commerce took over repairs in 1949, it kept the first nine letters to stand for the whole district and removed LAND.

02 **What was hidden on Wonderland Avenue?** Tap for the answer

Lookout Mountain Air Force Station, a classified film studio that produced thousands of military and atomic test films from 1947 to 1969. It is a private home today.

03 **How did buyers get up Laurel Canyon in 1910?** Tap for the answer

On a trackless trolley, an electric bus powered by overhead wires, which climbed from Sunset Boulevard for a dime.

04 **Which Beatles song is named for a street up here?** Tap for the answer

Blue Jay Way, one of the Bird Streets above the Sunset Strip. George Harrison wrote it there in August 1967.

05 **What did it cost to sponsor a letter in 1978?** Tap for the answer

About $27,700. Nine donors paid to replace the sign with steel letters that still stand on Mount Lee.

## The homes, the rules and who it fits

### The housing

Hillside homes on steep lots, from mid-century post-and-beam to new glass boxes. Expect hillside building limits, fire zone insurance, stairs and tight parking.

**Good fit if**

You want views and nightlife close by.

**Think twice if**

You hate stairs, hairpin turns or street parking.

Run the numbers [Mortgage](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/mortgage) [Rent vs buy](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/rent-vs-buy) [Transfer tax](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/transfer-tax/?city=los-angeles) [Compare](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/compare/?a=hollywood-hills&b=west-hollywood)

The rules here

- **Jurisdiction:** City of Los Angeles
- **Transfer tax:** 0.45% city + 0.11% county
- **Measure ULA:** Applies Yes. 4% of the full price over $5.4M, 5.5% at $10.9M and up (2026 thresholds)
- **Rent control:** LA's Rent Stabilization Ordinance covers most apartments in buildings built before October 1, 1978
- **Public schools:** Los Angeles Unified (LAUSD)

[Run the transfer tax](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/transfer-tax/?city=los-angeles) [Compare cities](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/la-rules)

Rules have exemptions. Confirm for a specific address.

What is Hollywood Hills like?

Runyon Canyon for the crowded hike, Lake Hollywood for the quiet loop, the Hollywood Bowl for summer nights, and Mulholland for the drive. You're up in the hills and still close to the Sunset Strip.

Is Hollywood Hills its own city?

Hollywood Hills is in City of Los Angeles. City and county rules apply.

What ZIP codes cover Hollywood Hills?

Hollywood Hills is mostly ZIP 90068, 90046, 90069.

West Third Street for shops and restaurants, Melrose Place for boutiques, La Cienega's restaurant row, and Cedars-Sinai as a major employer. It's central and very walkable.

## The pockets of Beverly Grove

[Every LA pocket on one map →](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/map)

In Los Angeles a single street can change the price of a house. Beverly Grove is really 5 smaller neighborhoods, and these are the lines between them, drawn street by street. Dashed outlines are the pockets next door.

### Melrose & Beverly Grove North

The West Hollywood line south to Beverly Boulevard, La Cienega to Fairfax

The Beverly Grove blocks between Melrose and Beverly: Spanish homes, duplexes and new builds near the Melrose shops.

### Burton Way & Cedars

Beverly Boulevard south to the Beverly Hills line, La Cienega west

Burton Way and Cedars: condo buildings along Burton Way and blocks around Cedars-Sinai and the Beverly Center.

### Beverly Grove

Beverly Boulevard to Wilshire, La Cienega to Fairfax

Beverly Grove: Spanish duplexes and homes around 3rd Street's shops and restaurants.

### Carthay Circle

Wilshire Boulevard to Olympic, La Cienega to Fairfax

Carthay Circle: a historic district of curving streets and Spanish homes, plus the blocks around it.

### South Carthay

Olympic Boulevard to Pico, La Cienega to Fairfax

South Carthay: a historic district of 1930s Spanish homes on a quiet grid.

The story of Beverly Grove

## Oil wells, a ballpark and the Farmers Market

Beverly Grove sits on the old Gilmore dairy ranch, where oil changed everything in the early 1900s. Earl Gilmore turned the family land into an entertainment district: a stadium for midget-car racing and football, a minor-league ballpark, a drive-in and, in 1934, a market where farmers sold produce off their trucks. Television City, The Grove and the Beverly Center all rose on the sites of those attractions.

3 min read 9 milestones 3 chapters 4 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1900s

Oil is struck on the Gilmore dairy ranch, founding the Gilmore Oil fortune.

- 1934

The Farmers Market opens at Third and Fairfax in July, and Gilmore Stadium opens next door in May.

- 1939

Gilmore Field opens, home of the Hollywood Stars baseball team.

- 1940

Gilmore Stadium hosts the NFL Pro Bowl.

- 1943

Beverly Park, a children's amusement park, opens at Beverly and La Cienega.

- 1952

CBS Television City opens on the site of Gilmore Stadium.

- 1958

Gilmore Field is torn down after the Stars leave town.

- 1974

Beverly Park closes. The Beverly Center opens on its site in 1982.

- 2002

The Grove opens on the site of the old Gilmore Drive-In.

IGilmore Island

### An entertainment district on an oil field

**1934** the Farmers Market opens

Arthur Gilmore ran a dairy here until oil came in, and his son Earl turned the family land into a playground for the growing city. Gilmore Stadium opened in 1934 for midget-car racing and football, Gilmore Field followed in 1939 as the home of the Pacific Coast League's Hollywood Stars, and a drive-in theater came later. In July 1934 a group of farmers began selling produce from their trucks on a Gilmore lot at Third and Fairfax. That was the beginning of the Farmers Market, which still has the feel of its first decades.

II1943 to 1974

### Kiddieland at Beverly and La Cienega

**31** years of Beverly Park

At the corner of Beverly and La Cienega, Beverly Park ran pony rides, a small roller coaster and a carousel for children from 1943 to 1974, popular with families from the nearby studios. When it closed, its site became the Beverly Center, which opened in 1982.

IIIWhat replaced them

### Television City and The Grove

**1952** Television City opens

CBS built Television City on the stadium site in 1952, and its studios have hosted decades of game shows, variety shows and specials. The ballpark became its parking lot after 1958, and the drive-in site became The Grove, which opened next to the Farmers Market in 2002. Walk the area today and almost every big landmark sits on top of a lost one.

## The homes, the rules and who it fits

### The housing

1920s and 1930s Spanish duplexes are the signature, along with single-family homes north of Beverly Boulevard and condos. Duplexes here work for owner-occupants who want rent from the second unit.

**Good fit if**

You want a central, walkable spot, or a duplex to live in and rent out.

**Think twice if**

You want a big backyard.

The rules here

- **Jurisdiction:** City of Los Angeles
- **Transfer tax:** 0.45% city + 0.11% county
- **Measure ULA:** Applies Yes. 4% of the full price over $5.4M, 5.5% at $10.9M and up (2026 thresholds)
- **Rent control:** LA's Rent Stabilization Ordinance covers most apartments in buildings built before October 1, 1978
- **Public schools:** Los Angeles Unified (LAUSD)

What it’s like

The Original Farmers Market has been at Third and Fairfax since 1934. The Grove is next door, Pan Pacific Park has fields and a rec center, Canter's Deli is open late, and Fairfax Avenue is a streetwear destination.

The Fairfax District is a City of LA neighborhood around Fairfax Avenue between Melrose and Wilshire, next to The Grove and CBS Television City.

The story of Fairfax District

## Delis, a market and a high school that started on a farm

Fairfax Avenue ran through farmland until the 1920s. Fairfax High opened in 1924 as an agricultural and mechanical school, the Farmers Market opened at Third and Fairfax in 1934, and after the Second World War delis, bakeries and bookstores moved west from Boyle Heights and turned the avenue into one of the most distinctive commercial strips in Los Angeles. Today it is also one of the world capitals of streetwear.

3 min read 7 milestones 3 chapters 4 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1924

Fairfax High School opens as an agricultural and mechanical school in a mostly rural corner of the city.

- 1934

The Farmers Market opens at Third and Fairfax.

- 1935

The streamline Pan-Pacific Auditorium opens on Beverly Boulevard.

- 1948

Canter's, founded in Boyle Heights in 1931, opens a location on Fairfax Avenue.

- 1953

Canter's moves into the former Esquire Theater at 419 N. Fairfax and starts staying open 24 hours.

- 1989

The long-closed Pan-Pacific Auditorium burns down. Its site is now Pan Pacific Park.

- 2000s

Skate and streetwear shops open on Fairfax, and lines around the block become a weekly sight.

IThe avenue moves west

### From Boyle Heights to Fairfax

**1931** Canter's opens in Boyle Heights

After the war, many families and businesses moved west from Boyle Heights, and Fairfax Avenue became their new main street. Canter's Deli, opened by the Canter brothers on Brooklyn Avenue in 1931, followed its customers to Fairfax in 1948 and in 1953 moved into a former movie theater at 419 N. Fairfax, where it began staying open around the clock. Bakeries, bookstores and delis lined the blocks between Beverly and Melrose, and many are still there.

II1935 to 1989

### The Pan-Pacific

**1935** the Pan-Pacific Auditorium opens

The Pan-Pacific Auditorium, with its streamline towers and flagpoles, opened in 1935 and hosted car shows, ice shows and political rallies for decades. It closed in 1972 and burned in 1989. The site is now Pan Pacific Park, whose recreation center nods to the streamline building that was one of the great examples of the style in America.

IIIToday

### Streetwear row

**24/7** Canter's hours since 1953

Starting in the 2000s, skate and streetwear brands opened stores on Fairfax, and the blocks north of Beverly became a destination for limited releases, with lines stretching down the sidewalk on drop days. The old delis and the new shops now share the same storefronts on the same few blocks.

Test yourself

03 **What happened to the Pan-Pacific Auditorium?** Tap for the answer

The story of Hancock Park & Larchmont

## Tar pits, oil wells and the houses they paid for

Hancock Park sits on the old Rancho La Brea, the land of the tar pits. The family that owned it pumped oil, dug up Ice Age bones, gave the fossils to the public and then, when the wells ran dry, built one of the grandest residential neighborhoods in the country. Its broad lawns, deep setbacks and period-revival houses are protected today almost exactly as they were built in the 1920s.

4 min read 11 milestones 4 chapters 4 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1863

Major Henry Hancock buys the eastern part of Rancho La Brea, the land around the tar pits.

- 1900

Oil leases turn the old rancho into a working oil field.

- 1911

Windsor Square opens to the east with its utilities placed underground from the start.

- 1913

G. Allan Hancock gives the county museum two years of exclusive digging rights at the tar pits.

- 1919

Residential development under the Hancock Park name begins as the oil wells decline.

- 1921

Julius LaBonte starts building the shops of Larchmont Village, the neighborhood's main street.

- 1924

Hancock donates 23 acres around the tar pits to LA County on condition that the fossils be preserved and shown.

- 1928

A Wallace Neff house is completed that later becomes the official residence of Britain's consul general.

- 1948

Nat King Cole buys a Tudor on Muirfield Road, months after the Supreme Court bars courts from enforcing racial covenants.

- 1977

Getty House in Windsor Square is donated to the city and becomes the official residence of the mayor.

- 2005

Windsor Square becomes a city historic district. Hancock Park is protected by its own HPOZ.

IRancho La Brea

### The land of the tar pits

**23** acres donated for the tar pits park

In 1863 Major Henry Hancock bought the eastern part of Rancho La Brea, the Spanish name for the tar that bubbled out of the ground there. Settlers had long used the tar to waterproof roofs. Oil wells followed around 1900, and while digging the family's workers kept finding bones.

Henry's son, G. Allan Hancock, recognized what they were. In 1913 he gave the county museum exclusive rights to excavate, and the pits gave up hundreds of thousands of Ice Age fossils, from saber-toothed cats to mammoths. In 1924 he donated 23 acres around the pits to the county on the condition that the fossils be preserved and displayed. That park on Wilshire still carries the family name and is the reason a neighborhood about a mile away shares it.

IIThe neighborhood

### From oil field to estate district

**1920s** when most of the houses were built

As the oil gave out, Hancock subdivided the land for homes, beginning around 1919. The lots were large, the setbacks deep and the front lawns open to the street, and buyers commissioned Tudor, English and Spanish Revival, Colonial and Mediterranean houses from the leading architects of the 1920s. The Wilshire Country Club anchors the western side.

Next door, Windsor Square had opened in 1911 with its power lines buried underground. Its best-known house, Getty House on Irving Boulevard, was donated to the city in 1977 and is now the official home of the mayor of Los Angeles. To the east, Julius LaBonte began building the storefronts of Larchmont Boulevard in 1921, a small-town main street created to serve the new neighborhoods, and it still plays that role.

III1948

### Nat King Cole on Muirfield Road

**1948** Shelley v. Kraemer ends court enforcement of covenants

Like many Los Angeles neighborhoods of its era, Hancock Park was built with deed covenants that barred sales to Black buyers. In May 1948 the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in Shelley v. Kraemer that courts could no longer enforce them. That August, singer Nat King Cole bought a Tudor house on Muirfield Road.

The local property owners association tried to stop the purchase and pressed him to sell. Cole refused and raised his family in the house. The episode is now taught as a turning point in the city's housing history, and fair housing law today protects every buyer's right to live wherever they choose.

IVPreservation

### Why it still looks like 1925

**HPOZ** historic overlay protects the streetscape

Hancock Park and Windsor Square are both covered by Historic Preservation Overlay Zones, the city's version of historic districts. Exterior changes visible from the street go through design review, which keeps the lawns open, the rooflines intact and new construction in scale with the old. For owners it is a trade: more process for renovations, and a streetscape that cannot be lost.

Test yourself

### Did you know?

01 **Why is the tar pits park called Hancock Park too?** Tap for the answer

G. Allan Hancock donated the land around the tar pits to LA County in 1924. The neighborhood he developed nearby carries the same family name.

02 **Where does the mayor of Los Angeles live?** Tap for the answer

Getty House on Irving Boulevard in Windsor Square, donated to the city in 1977.

03 **What does La Brea mean?** Tap for the answer

The tar. Spanish settlers named the rancho for the natural asphalt that seeps up from the ground.

04 **Why do so few houses here have front walls or tall hedges?** Tap for the answer

Open front lawns were part of the original 1920s plan, and the historic overlay protects that look today.

Living here

## The homes, the rules and who it fits

### The housing

1920s Tudor, Spanish and Colonial estates. Hancock Park is an HPOZ, so exterior changes go through historic review.

**Good fit if**

You want an old-LA house on a quiet, walkable street.

**Think twice if**

You want a modern build with no review process.

Run the numbers [Mortgage](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/mortgage) [Rent vs buy](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/rent-vs-buy) [Transfer tax](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/transfer-tax/?city=los-angeles) [Compare](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/compare/?a=hancock-park&b=miracle-mile)

The rules here

- **Jurisdiction:** City of Los Angeles
- **Transfer tax:** 0.45% city + 0.11% county
- **Measure ULA:** Applies Yes. 4% of the full price over $5.4M, 5.5% at $10.9M and up (2026 thresholds)
- **Rent control:** LA's Rent Stabilization Ordinance covers most apartments in buildings built before October 1, 1978
- **Public schools:** Los Angeles Unified (LAUSD)

[Run the transfer tax](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/transfer-tax/?city=los-angeles) [Compare cities](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/la-rules)

Rules have exemptions. Confirm for a specific address.

# Hollywood

Studios, nightlife and the B Line. Live a few blocks off the boulevard.

City of LA ZIP 90028, 90038 $$ · Moderate

Get Hollywood listings What's my Hollywood home worth?

What it’s like

Busy and loud around Hollywood and Highland, calmer on the side streets. The Hollywood Bowl, Hollywood Forever's summer movies, and studios like Paramount keep it a working entertainment neighborhood.

Hollywood is the City of LA neighborhood around Hollywood Boulevard and Sunset, with Paramount Pictures on Melrose and Metro B Line stations under the boulevard.

[Nightlife](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/#nightlife) [Near Metro rail](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/#transit) [Condo friendly](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/#condo) [Creative](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/#creative) [More for the money](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/#value)

Block by block

## The pockets of Hollywood

[Every LA pocket on one map →](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/map)

In Los Angeles a single street can change the price of a house. Hollywood is really 6 smaller neighborhoods, and these are the lines between them, drawn street by street. Dashed outlines are the pockets next door.

### Spaulding Square

The West Hollywood line north to Sunset, Fairfax to La Brea

Spaulding Square and its neighbors: 1920s bungalows and Spanish homes, partly a historic district.

### Sunset Square

Sunset Boulevard to Hollywood Boulevard, Fairfax to La Brea

Sunset Square: a historic district of 1920s homes and duplexes at the foot of the hills.

### Central Hollywood

Sunset Boulevard to Franklin, La Brea to the Hollywood Freeway

Central Hollywood: the Walk of Fame, high-rise living and older apartment buildings.

### Franklin Village

Sunset Boulevard to Franklin, the Hollywood Freeway to Western

Franklin Village and the east side of central Hollywood: older apartments, small homes and the Franklin Avenue cafes.

### Hollywood Media District

Santa Monica Boulevard to Sunset, La Brea to Western

Hollywood's media district: studios and post-production houses, apartments and a few small-home streets.

### Hollywood Studio District

Melrose Avenue to Santa Monica Boulevard, La Brea to Western

The studio district between Melrose and Santa Monica: small homes and duplexes near Paramount and the Hollywood Forever cemetery.

The story of Hollywood

## From a quiet suburb to the movie capital of the world

Hollywood was named by Daeida Wilcox, whose husband Harvey subdivided a ranch here in 1887 as an orderly, tree-lined suburb. It became a city in 1903, gave up its independence to Los Angeles for water in 1910, and that same decade the filmmakers arrived. Within twenty years the name meant movies everywhere on earth.

3 min read 10 milestones 3 chapters 5 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1887

Harvey Wilcox files a subdivision map, and his wife Daeida names it Hollywood.

- 1903

Hollywood incorporates as a city.

- 1910

Hollywood merges with Los Angeles to get water.

- 1911

Nestor Studios opens the first film studio in Hollywood at Sunset and Gower.

- 1914

Cecil B. DeMille shoots The Squaw Man in a barn near Selma and Vine.

- 1922

Grauman's Egyptian Theatre opens on Hollywood Boulevard.

- 1927

Grauman's Chinese Theatre and the Hollywood Roosevelt Hotel open.

- 1929

The first Academy Awards are handed out at the Roosevelt on May 16.

- 1956

The Capitol Records Tower is completed.

- 1960

The first stars are installed on the Walk of Fame.

I1887

### The Wilcoxes' town

**1903** Hollywood incorporates

Harvey and Daeida Wilcox subdivided their ranch below the hills in 1887, and Daeida gave it the name Hollywood. It grew into a quiet suburb of orchards and churches, incorporated in 1903, and seven years later voted to join Los Angeles because it needed the city's water.

II1911

### The movies arrive

**1911** the first Hollywood studio

In 1911 the Nestor company opened the first film studio in Hollywood at Sunset and Gower, and the rest of the industry followed for the sunshine, cheap land and varied scenery. In 1914 Cecil B. DeMille made The Squaw Man in a horse barn near Selma and Vine. That barn, moved twice since, is now the Hollywood Heritage Museum across from the Hollywood Bowl.

IIIThe boulevard

### Palaces, premieres and the Walk of Fame

**15 min** length of the first Oscars ceremony

Showman Sid Grauman built the Egyptian Theatre in 1922 and the Chinese Theatre in 1927, where stars began leaving hand and footprints in the forecourt. The Hollywood Roosevelt opened the same year and hosted the first Academy Awards in 1929, a dinner where the awards took about 15 minutes. Capitol Records finished its round tower in 1956, and the Walk of Fame's first stars went in in 1960.

## The homes, the rules and who it fits

### The housing

Apartments and condos, 1920s bungalow courts, and historic pockets like Spaulding Square. Lots of rental stock under rent stabilization.

**Good fit if**

You want energy, a train and to be close to the studios.

**Think twice if**

You want quiet streets.

Run the numbers [Mortgage](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/mortgage) [Rent vs buy](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/rent-vs-buy) [Transfer tax](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/transfer-tax/?city=los-angeles) [Compare](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/compare/?a=hollywood&b=hollywood-hills)

The rules here

- **Jurisdiction:** City of Los Angeles
- **Transfer tax:** 0.45% city + 0.11% county
- **Measure ULA:** Applies Yes. 4% of the full price over $5.4M, 5.5% at $10.9M and up (2026 thresholds)
- **Rent control:** LA's Rent Stabilization Ordinance covers most apartments in buildings built before October 1, 1978
- **Public schools:** Los Angeles Unified (LAUSD)

What it’s like

Museums at your door, Park La Brea's towers, and Metro D Line subway stations on Wilshire. The residential streets south of Wilshire are calm and walkable.

Miracle Mile is the City of LA neighborhood along Wilshire Boulevard between Fairfax and La Brea, home to LACMA, the Academy Museum, the Petersen and the La Brea Tar Pits.

## The pockets of Miracle Mile

[Every LA pocket on one map →](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/map)

In Los Angeles a single street can change the price of a house. Miracle Mile is really 2 smaller neighborhoods, and these are the lines between them, drawn street by street. Dashed outlines are the pockets next door.

### Museum Row

6th Street to Wilshire Boulevard, Fairfax to La Brea

Museum Row: LACMA, the Academy Museum and the La Brea Tar Pits, with apartments and condos north of Wilshire.
