The story of Miracle Mile

## The first shopping street built for the car

In 1921 developer A.W. Ross bought land along a dirt stretch of Wilshire Boulevard and bet that Angelenos would drive, not walk, to shop. He built storefronts scaled to be read through a windshield, with parking behind them, and the strip became the Miracle Mile. Its Art Deco department stores now hold museums, and the tar pits next door are still giving up Ice Age fossils.

3 min read 9 milestones 2 chapters 4 landmarks

### Timeline

- Ice Age

Animals from mammoths to saber-toothed cats are trapped in the asphalt seeps of Rancho La Brea.

- 1921

A.W. Ross buys land on Wilshire Boulevard for a shopping district designed around the automobile.

- 1924

G. Allan Hancock donates the tar pits and 23 acres to LA County as a park.

- 1939

The May Company department store opens at Wilshire and Fairfax, with its gold-tiled corner cylinder.

- 1940s

Park La Brea, a planned apartment community, rises just north of Wilshire.

- 1965

The Los Angeles County Museum of Art opens on Wilshire.

- 1977

The Page Museum opens at the tar pits.

- 1994

The Petersen Automotive Museum opens in a former department store.

- 2021

The Academy Museum of Motion Pictures opens in the old May Company building.

I1921

### Built for the windshield

**1921** A.W. Ross buys on Wilshire

A.W. Ross noticed that Los Angeles was spreading west faster than the streetcars could follow, and that shoppers would soon arrive by car. On a quiet stretch of Wilshire between La Brea and Fairfax he planned stores with big signs and bold facades meant to be seen at 30 miles an hour, with parking lots behind them. Downtown merchants scoffed. The strip boomed, and the name Miracle Mile stuck.

IIMuseum Row

### Department stores become museums

**1939** the May Company building opens

The great Streamline and Art Deco stores of the Miracle Mile lost their shoppers to malls in the late twentieth century, and museums moved in. LACMA opened in 1965, the Petersen Automotive Museum took over a former department store in 1994, and the gold-cylindered May Company building of 1939 reopened in 2021 as the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures. The La Brea Tar Pits, still an active dig site, sit in the middle of it all.

01 **Why is it called the Miracle Mile?** Tap for the answer

Because a dirt stretch of Wilshire turned into a booming shopping district designed for drivers in just a few years after 1921.

02 **What is inside the old May Company building?** Tap for the answer

The Academy Museum of Motion Pictures, which opened there in 2021.

03 **Are scientists still digging at the tar pits?** Tap for the answer

Yes. La Brea is an active excavation site in the middle of the city.

## The homes, the rules and who it fits

### The housing

1920s and 1930s duplexes and single-family homes, much of it inside the Miracle Mile HPOZ, plus condos on Wilshire and the Park La Brea apartments.

**Good fit if**

You want culture and a subway stop in walking distance.

**Think twice if**

You want to change a historic facade.

The rules here

- **Jurisdiction:** City of Los Angeles
- **Transfer tax:** 0.45% city + 0.11% county
- **Measure ULA:** Applies Yes. 4% of the full price over $5.4M, 5.5% at $10.9M and up (2026 thresholds)
- **Rent control:** LA's Rent Stabilization Ordinance covers most apartments in buildings built before October 1, 1978
- **Public schools:** Los Angeles Unified (LAUSD)

What it’s like

The Sunset Strip's music venues, the Rainbow District's nightlife on Santa Monica Boulevard, the Design District around Melrose and Robertson, and very walkable residential streets in between.

## The pockets of West Hollywood

In Los Angeles a single street can change the price of a house. West Hollywood is really 7 smaller neighborhoods, and these are the lines between them, drawn street by street. Dashed outlines are the pockets next door.

### West Hollywood West

Santa Monica Boulevard south to the city line at Beverly, Doheny Drive to La Cienega

West Hollywood West: a quiet grid of Spanish homes, duplexes and new builds next to the Pacific Design Center and Robertson.

### Norma Triangle

Santa Monica Boulevard to Sunset, Doheny Drive to San Vicente

Norma Triangle: small streets of cottages and duplexes in the triangle below Sunset, a short walk to both the Strip and Santa Monica Boulevard.

### Sunset Strip

The West Hollywood side of Sunset Boulevard, Doheny to Crescent Heights

The Sunset Strip: the boulevard itself and the city's thin band of hillside lots just above it.

### West Hollywood Center

Santa Monica Boulevard to Sunset, San Vicente to La Cienega

Central West Hollywood: apartments, condos and small homes around Santa Monica Boulevard's busiest stretch.

### West Hollywood North

Santa Monica Boulevard to Sunset and the city line, La Cienega to Fairfax

West Hollywood north of Santa Monica Boulevard: historic courtyard buildings, condos and homes around Havenhurst, Harper and Kings Road.

### West Hollywood South

Santa Monica Boulevard south to the city line, La Cienega to Fairfax

West Hollywood south of Santa Monica Boulevard: Spanish duplexes, small homes and new builds up to the city line near Melrose.

### West Hollywood Eastside

Fairfax Avenue to the city line at La Brea

West Hollywood's Eastside: apartments and condos around Plummer Park and the Formosa and Gardner streets.

The story of West Hollywood

## The railroad town that became the Sunset Strip

West Hollywood began as Sherman, a yard town for Moses Sherman's electric railway. Because it stayed outside the Los Angeles city limits, its stretch of Sunset Boulevard became the Sunset Strip, home to nightclubs beyond the reach of the city's police, then to rock clubs, and finally to a city of its own, incorporated in 1984.

3 min read 10 milestones 3 chapters 5 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1890s

The town of Sherman grows around the rail yards of Moses Sherman's Los Angeles Pacific Railroad.

- 1922

Architect Rudolph Schindler builds his concrete-and-glass house on Kings Road.

- 1925

Sherman renames itself West Hollywood.

- 1929

The Chateau Marmont opens above Sunset.

- 1930s-40s

The Trocadero, Ciro's and the Mocambo make the Strip the nightlife capital of Hollywood.

- 1957

The Troubadour opens on Santa Monica Boulevard.

- 1964

The Whisky a Go Go opens on the Strip.

- 1966

Young people protest a curfew in what became known as the Sunset Strip riots.

- 1975

The Pacific Design Center, the Blue Whale, opens.

- 1984

West Hollywood incorporates as a city on November 29.

ISherman

### A railroad town

**1925** Sherman becomes West Hollywood

The flats along Santa Monica Boulevard grew up as Sherman, where the Los Angeles Pacific Railroad kept its yards and shops. As Hollywood became famous, the town traded its name for West Hollywood in 1925. Its streets of bungalows and courtyard apartments date largely from those years.

IIThe Strip

### Outside the city limits

**1.5 mi** of Sunset Boulevard on the Strip

Because West Hollywood was unincorporated county land, the curving stretch of Sunset between Hollywood and Beverly Hills fell outside the Los Angeles Police Department's reach. In the 1930s and 1940s that made it the place for glamorous nightclubs like the Trocadero, Ciro's and the Mocambo, where studio stars were photographed every night. The Chateau Marmont, opened in 1929, became the hideaway hotel above it all.

IIIRock and roll

### From the Whisky to a city

**1984** West Hollywood incorporates

In the 1960s the supper clubs gave way to rock clubs. The Whisky a Go Go opened in 1964, and the Strip became a launching pad for bands from the Doors on. In 1966 crowds of young people protesting a curfew clashed with police, an episode remembered as the Sunset Strip riots. Residents voted to incorporate in 1984, and West Hollywood has since become one of the densest and most walkable cities in the county, anchored by the bright blue and green glass of the Pacific Design Center.

## The homes, the rules and who it fits

### The housing

Condos, rent-stabilized apartments, small houses in the Norma Triangle and on the east side, and hillside homes above Sunset.

**Good fit if**

You want to walk to dinner and stay out late.

**Think twice if**

You want a yard or a quiet Saturday night.

# East Hollywood

Thai Town, Little Armenia and Barnsdall Park, right on the B Line.

City of LA ZIP 90029 $$ · Moderate

Get East Hollywood listings What's my East Hollywood home worth?

What it’s like

Barnsdall Art Park holds Frank Lloyd Wright's Hollyhock House, a UNESCO World Heritage site. Thai Town's restaurants line Hollywood Boulevard, and the hospital row on Sunset and Vermont is a major employer.

East Hollywood is a City of LA neighborhood between Hollywood, Los Feliz and Silver Lake. It includes Thai Town and Little Armenia, and Metro B Line stations at Vermont.

## The pockets of East Hollywood

In Los Angeles a single street can change the price of a house. East Hollywood is really 3 smaller neighborhoods, and these are the lines between them, drawn street by street. Dashed outlines are the pockets next door.

### Thai Town & Little Armenia

Hollywood Boulevard to Santa Monica Boulevard, Western to Vermont

Thai Town and Little Armenia: apartments and small homes along Hollywood Boulevard's restaurant strip.

### Melrose Hill & East Hollywood South

Santa Monica Boulevard to Melrose, Western to Vermont

The south half of East Hollywood: bungalows and duplexes, including the small Melrose Hill historic district.

### Virgil Village & Barnsdall

Hollywood Boulevard and Sunset south to Melrose, Vermont to Hoover

Virgil Village and Barnsdall: craftsman bungalows and small apartments near Barnsdall Art Park and the Vermont hospitals.

## Where to eat, drink and go in East Hollywood

See them on the map →

East Hollywood takes in Thai Town, Little Armenia, Virgil Village and the Melrose Hill strip, between Hollywood and Los Feliz. It is one of the deepest eating neighborhoods in LA, with some of the city's best Thai cooking, a run of chef-driven spots on Melrose and a few great small bars.

The story of East Hollywood

## UCLA's first campus and Frank Lloyd Wright's Hollyhock House

East Hollywood is where Los Angeles went to college. The state normal school moved to Vermont Avenue in 1914, became the first home of UCLA in 1919 and, when UCLA left for Westwood in 1929, Los Angeles City College. Up the hill, oil heiress Aline Barnsdall commissioned Frank Lloyd Wright's first Los Angeles house, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and along Hollywood Boulevard the city designated Thai Town and Little Armenia.

3 min read 8 milestones 3 chapters 3 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1914

The Los Angeles State Normal School, a teachers college, moves from downtown to Vermont Avenue.

- 1919

The Southern Branch of the University of California, later UCLA, opens on the Vermont campus on September 15.

- 1921

Frank Lloyd Wright completes Hollyhock House for Aline Barnsdall on Olive Hill.

- 1927

Barnsdall gives the house and hilltop to the city. It is now Barnsdall Art Park.

- 1929

UCLA moves to Westwood, and Los Angeles Junior College opens on the old campus in September. It is renamed Los Angeles City College in 1938.

- 1999

The city designates Thai Town along Hollywood Boulevard.

- 2000

The city designates Little Armenia on October 6.

- 2019

Hollyhock House is inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

IVermont Avenue

### UCLA's first home

**76-0** UCLA's score against USC in the first game, 1929

In 1914 the state normal school, which trained teachers, moved to a new Romanesque campus on Vermont Avenue. In 1919 it became the Southern Branch of the University of California, the school that grew into UCLA. Within ten years it had outgrown the site and moved to Westwood. The Board of Education bought the Vermont campus for $700,000, and Los Angeles Junior College opened there in September 1929. It became Los Angeles City College in 1938.

IIOlive Hill

### Hollyhock House

**2019** UNESCO World Heritage listing

Oil heiress Aline Barnsdall bought Olive Hill to build an arts colony and hired Frank Lloyd Wright to design her house. Finished in 1921 and decorated with stylized hollyhocks, her favorite flower, it was Wright's first commission in Los Angeles. Barnsdall gave the house and the hilltop to the city in 1927, and in 2019 Hollyhock House joined seven other Wright buildings on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

IIIHollywood Boulevard east

### Thai Town and Little Armenia

**1999** Thai Town is designated

East of the 101, Hollywood Boulevard is lined with restaurants, markets, bakeries and churches. The city formally recognized the stretch as Thai Town in 1999, the first such designation in the country, and the blocks around it as Little Armenia in 2000.

## The homes, the rules and who it fits

### The housing

Apartments, duplexes, bungalows and some of the most attainable houses this close to Los Feliz and Silver Lake. Much of the rental stock is under rent stabilization.

**Good fit if**

You want value next to the Eastside's best neighborhoods.

**Think twice if**

The rules here

- **Jurisdiction:** City of Los Angeles
- **Transfer tax:** 0.45% city + 0.11% county
- **Measure ULA:** Applies Yes. 4% of the full price over $5.4M, 5.5% at $10.9M and up (2026 thresholds)
- **Rent control:** LA's Rent Stabilization Ordinance covers most apartments in buildings built before October 1, 1978
- **Public schools:** Los Angeles Unified (LAUSD)

Echo Park Lake with the paddle boats and lotus beds, Dodger Stadium up the hill, Elysian Park's trails, and a strip of bars, music venues and restaurants on Sunset.

The hills north of Echo Park Avenue toward Elysian Park

Elysian Heights: hillside homes and stairways bordering Elysian Park.

### Echo Park Avenue

Echo Park Avenue and the streets around Lemoyne and Logan

Echo Park Avenue: hillside bungalows and small apartment buildings north of Sunset.

The streets around Echo Park Lake

Echo Park Lake: homes and apartments around the lake and its lotus beds.

The streets around Carroll Avenue and Kensington Road

Angelino Heights: one of LA's first suburbs, known for its Victorian homes on Carroll Avenue.

The hill streets east of Echo Park near Chinatown

Victor Heights: a small hillside pocket between Echo Park, Chinatown and Dodger Stadium.

The story of Echo Park

## Edendale, a lake that echoes and Sister Aimee's temple

Before Hollywood, there was Edendale. In the 1910s silent-film studios lined what is now Glendale Boulevard, and the neighborhood's lake, dug as a reservoir in 1868, was rebuilt as a park in 1892 by a parks superintendent who named it for the echoes he heard. In 1923 Aimee Semple McPherson opened Angelus Temple on its shore, and in 1962 Dodger Stadium opened on the hill above.

3 min read 9 milestones 3 chapters 5 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1868

Reservoir No. 4 is created, fed by a ditch from the Los Angeles River.

- 1886

Elysian Park, the city's oldest public park, is established next door.

- 1891

Landowners give the city 33 acres around the reservoir for a park.

- 1892

Work on the park begins, and superintendent Joseph Henry Tomlinson names it Echo Park.

- 1909

William Selig opens what is often called the first permanent movie studio in Los Angeles, in Edendale.

- 1912

Mack Sennett's Keystone studio opens on Allesandro Street, now Glendale Boulevard.

- 1923

Angelus Temple opens on January 1.

- 1962

Dodger Stadium opens in Chavez Ravine.

- 2013

Echo Park Lake reopens after a two-year restoration.

IEdendale

### Hollywood before Hollywood

**1909** the Selig studio opens

In 1909 William Selig built a permanent film studio in Edendale, the old name for the area along today's Glendale Boulevard, and others followed, including Mack Sennett's Keystone studio, home of the Keystone Kops. For a few years this was the center of West Coast filmmaking. Sennett's old studio building still stands at 1712 Glendale Boulevard, a city monument.

II1892

### The lake that echoes

**1868** the reservoir is dug

Echo Park Lake started in 1868 as Reservoir No. 4, filled by a ditch from the Los Angeles River. When the city turned it into a park in 1892, parks superintendent Joseph Henry Tomlinson named it for the echoes he heard while crews worked. The lotus beds that bloom each summer are the reason for the annual Lotus Festival.

III1923 and 1962

### A temple and a ballpark

**5,300** seats in Angelus Temple

On January 1, 1923, evangelist Aimee Semple McPherson opened Angelus Temple on the lake's north shore, a domed church that drew thousands of people to the neighborhood and broadcast on its own radio station. Four decades later the Dodgers opened their stadium in Chavez Ravine on the hill above, and Echo Park has been the walk to the game ever since.

Parks superintendent Joseph Henry Tomlinson named it in 1892 for the echoes he heard during construction.

02 **Was the lake always a lake?** Tap for the answer

No. It began in 1868 as a drinking water reservoir.

03 **Where were Keystone Kops movies made?** Tap for the answer

At Mack Sennett's studio on what is now Glendale Boulevard in Edendale.

The rules here

- **Jurisdiction:** City of Los Angeles
- **Transfer tax:** 0.45% city + 0.11% county
- **Measure ULA:** Applies Yes. 4% of the full price over $5.4M, 5.5% at $10.9M and up (2026 thresholds)
- **Rent control:** LA's Rent Stabilization Ordinance covers most apartments in buildings built before October 1, 1978
- **Public schools:** Los Angeles Unified (LAUSD)

# Los Feliz

Griffith Park as a backyard and Vermont Avenue for dinner.

City of LA ZIP 90027 $$$$ · Top of market

Get Los Feliz listings What's my Los Feliz home worth?

What it’s like

Los Feliz Village on Vermont and Hillhurst has the restaurants, bars and bookstores. The park has hiking, golf, the zoo and the observatory. Frank Lloyd Wright's Ennis House sits on the hill.

Los Feliz is a City of LA neighborhood at the foot of Griffith Park, one of the largest city parks in the country, with the Griffith Observatory and the Greek Theatre in the hills above.

Block by block

## The pockets of Los Feliz

[Every LA pocket on one map →](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/map)

In Los Angeles a single street can change the price of a house. Los Feliz is really 6 smaller neighborhoods, and these are the lines between them, drawn street by street. Dashed outlines are the pockets next door.

### Los Feliz Flats

Los Feliz Boulevard to Hollywood Boulevard, Western to Vermont, around Laughlin Park

The Los Feliz flats: Spanish and Tudor homes and classic apartment buildings on a tree-lined grid.

### Laughlin Park

Franklin Avenue to Los Feliz Boulevard, Hobart to Normandie

Laughlin Park: a small gated hill of historic estates above Franklin Avenue.

### Los Feliz Village

Los Feliz Boulevard to Hollywood Boulevard, Vermont to Hillhurst

Los Feliz Village: the shops and cafes of Vermont and Hillhurst, with homes and apartments between them.

### Los Feliz Estates

North of Los Feliz Boulevard, west of Vermont toward Fern Dell

Los Feliz Estates: hillside homes north of the boulevard near the Griffith Park entrance at Fern Dell.

### Los Feliz Oaks

North of Los Feliz Boulevard around Glendower, Bryn Mawr and Commonwealth

Los Feliz Oaks: large hillside homes, including the Ennis House, on the slopes below Griffith Observatory.

### Franklin Hills

Hillhurst east to Hyperion, Los Feliz Boulevard south to Sunset

Franklin Hills: hillside homes and public stairways around the Shakespeare Bridge.

The story of Los Feliz

## Griffith's gift and the hillside of landmark houses

Los Feliz takes its name from Rancho Los Feliz. In 1896 Griffith J. Griffith gave Los Angeles more than 3,000 acres of it for a park, and the hillsides below filled with some of the most important houses in America, including a Frank Lloyd Wright temple of textile blocks and a Richard Neutra house that announced modern architecture to the country. Walt Disney started his first Los Angeles studio a few blocks away.

3 min read 8 milestones 3 chapters 5 landmarks

### Timeline

- Rancho era

The land is Rancho Los Feliz, granted to the family of Jose Vicente Feliz.

- 1896

Griffith J. Griffith donates 3,015 acres to the city for Griffith Park.

- 1923

Walt and Roy Disney start their studio on Kingswell Avenue.

- 1924

Frank Lloyd Wright's Ennis House is completed on the hill above Los Feliz Boulevard.

- 1929

Richard Neutra's Lovell Health House, a steel-framed modern house, is finished.

- 1930

The Greek Theatre opens in Griffith Park.

- 1935

Griffith Observatory opens.

- 1940

The Mulholland Memorial Fountain is dedicated at Riverside and Los Feliz.

I1896

### Griffith's gift

**3,015** acres donated for Griffith Park

Griffith J. Griffith, a mining speculator, bought part of the old Rancho Los Feliz and in 1896 gave 3,015 acres of it to Los Angeles for a public park. His will later paid for the Greek Theatre and the Griffith Observatory, which opened in 1935 with the promise that anyone could look through its telescopes for free. Admission to the observatory is still free.

IIThe hillside

### Houses that changed architecture

**1924** Ennis House

The slopes below the park became a showcase. Frank Lloyd Wright's Ennis House of 1924, built of patterned concrete blocks, looks like a Mayan temple and has appeared in films from Blade Runner on. Five years later Richard Neutra finished the Lovell Health House, a steel frame hung with glass and concrete on a steep lot, one of the first fully modern houses in the United States. Both are on the hills above Los Feliz Boulevard.

III1923

### Where Disney began

**1923** Disney's first LA studio

In 1923 Walt Disney and his brother Roy set up shop on Kingswell Avenue, first in an uncle's garage and then in a small storefront nearby. They moved to a bigger studio on Hyperion Avenue in Silver Lake in 1926, but Los Feliz is where the company that would make Mickey Mouse began.

Test yourself

02 **Which famous house looks like a Mayan temple?** Tap for the answer

03 **Where did Walt Disney start his studio?** Tap for the answer

## The homes, the rules and who it fits

### The housing

1920s Spanish and Tudor homes on the flats, estates in Los Feliz Oaks, Laughlin Park and the Los Feliz Estates hills, and apartments near Vermont.

**Good fit if**

You want a walkable village and a huge park at your door.

**Think twice if**

You need to be on the Westside every day.

The rules here

- **Jurisdiction:** City of Los Angeles
- **Transfer tax:** 0.45% city + 0.11% county
- **Measure ULA:** Applies Yes. 4% of the full price over $5.4M, 5.5% at $10.9M and up (2026 thresholds)
- **Rent control:** LA's Rent Stabilization Ordinance covers most apartments in buildings built before October 1, 1978
- **Public schools:** Los Angeles Unified (LAUSD)

What is Los Feliz like?

Los Feliz Village on Vermont and Hillhurst has the restaurants, bars and bookstores. The park has hiking, golf, the zoo and the observatory. Frank Lloyd Wright's Ennis House sits on the hill.

Los Feliz is in City of Los Angeles. City and county rules apply.

What ZIP codes cover Los Feliz?

Los Feliz is mostly ZIP 90027.

What kind of homes are in Los Feliz?

1920s Spanish and Tudor homes on the flats, estates in Los Feliz Oaks, Laughlin Park and the Los Feliz Estates hills, and apartments near Vermont.

What is the transfer tax when you sell in Los Feliz?

0.45% city + 0.11% county

Does rent control apply in Los Feliz?

LA's Rent Stabilization Ordinance covers most apartments in buildings built before October 1, 1978

# Silver Lake

The reservoir loop, Sunset Junction and modernist houses on the hills.

City of LA ZIP 90026, 90039 $$$ · Upper

Get Silver Lake listings What's my Silver Lake home worth?

What it’s like

The reservoir walking path and the Meadow on weekends, Sunset Junction's coffee and shops, public stairways through the hills, and some of LA's best modern architecture by Neutra, Schindler and Lautner.

Silver Lake is a City of LA neighborhood built around the Silver Lake Reservoir, between Los Feliz and Echo Park.

The story of Silver Lake

## A reservoir, a famous staircase and Disney's first big studio

Silver Lake is named for a reservoir, and the reservoir for Herman Silver, a member of the city's water board. Around it grew Walt Disney's first big studio, a staircase made famous by Laurel and Hardy, and hillsides where Richard Neutra and a generation of modern architects built.

3 min read 7 milestones 3 chapters 4 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1907

The Silver Lake Reservoir is completed and named for water commissioner Herman Silver.

- 1926

Walt Disney moves his studio to Hyperion Avenue.

- 1932

Laurel and Hardy haul a piano up the Vendome Street stairs in The Music Box, which wins an Academy Award.

- 1932

Richard Neutra builds his VDL Research House on the reservoir.

- 1937

Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, made at the Hyperion studio, premieres.

- 1940

Disney moves to Burbank.

- 1967

Patrons of the Black Cat Tavern protest a police raid, two years before Stonewall.

I1907

### The reservoir

**1907** the reservoir is completed

The Silver Lake Reservoir was built in 1907 to store water for a growing city and named for Herman Silver, a member of the water board. The hills around it filled with houses in the 1920s and 1930s, and the walking path around the water and the meadow beside it are now the neighborhood's front yard.

II1926 to 1940

### Disney on Hyperion

**1937** Snow White premieres

In 1926 Walt Disney moved his young studio to Hyperion Avenue, and over the next 14 years it produced Mickey Mouse cartoons and the first full-length animated feature, Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs. Disney moved to Burbank in 1940, and the Hyperion site is now a supermarket. A few blocks away, Laurel and Hardy filmed The Music Box on a long public staircase off Vendome Street in 1932, and the steps still carry the film's name.

IIIModern hills

### Neutra and the modernists

**1932** Neutra's VDL Research House

Richard Neutra built his own house and studio on the reservoir in 1932 and later designed a cluster of houses nearby along Silver Lake Boulevard. Rudolph Schindler, John Lautner and others built on the surrounding hills, making Silver Lake one of the densest collections of modern houses in the country.

The story of Encino

## The valley of the oaks

Encino is where the Spanish first named the San Fernando Valley. In 1769 the Portola expedition camped by a spring here and called the whole valley Santa Catalina de Bononia de los Encinos, the valley of the oaks. The spring still flows in Los Encinos State Historic Park beside an 1849 adobe, and a live oak more than 1,000 years old stood nearby until a storm brought it down in 1998.

3 min read 9 milestones 3 chapters 3 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1769

The Portola expedition camps at the spring and names the valley for its oaks.

- 1797

Mission San Fernando is founded. Its padres had used Encino as a base while exploring the valley.

- 1845

Rancho El Encino is granted to three Native Californians: Roman, Roque and Francisco.

- 1849

Vicente de la Ossa builds a nine-room adobe beside the spring.

- 1872

Eugene Garnier builds a two-story limestone house on the rancho.

- 1941

Sepulveda Dam is completed, creating the Sepulveda Basin.

- 1949

The adobe, spring and Garnier house become Los Encinos State Historic Park.

- 1963

The great Encino Oak is named a city monument.

- 1998

The 1,000-year-old oak falls in a February storm.

I1769

### Portola's spring

**1769** Encino names the Valley

When the Spanish expedition led by Gaspar de Portola crossed into the valley in August 1769, it camped beside a spring among great oaks and gave the whole valley a name that honored them. Encino is Spanish for live oak. The spring still feeds a pond at Los Encinos State Historic Park on Ventura Boulevard.

IIRancho El Encino

### An adobe on the old road

**9** rooms in the 1849 adobe

In 1845 the land was granted to three Native Californians. Vicente de la Ossa bought in and built a nine-room adobe in 1849 that served travelers on the road through the valley, and Eugene Garnier added a two-story limestone house in 1872. The state bought the last parcel with the spring and both buildings in 1949. They were heavily damaged in the 1994 earthquake and restored.

III1998

### The Lang Oak

**1,000+** years old when it fell

The Encino Oak, also called the Lang Oak, was already centuries old when Portola passed by. Its branches spread about 150 feet. It was named a city Historic-Cultural Monument in 1963 and fell during a storm in February 1998, mourned by neighbors who came to say goodbye.

03 **What is at Los Encinos State Historic Park?** Tap for the answer

An 1849 adobe, an 1872 limestone house, a blacksmith shop and the natural spring.

The story of North Hollywood

## Toluca, then Lankershim, then NoHo

North Hollywood has had three names. It started as Toluca, became Lankershim in honor of the family that owned the valley floor, and in 1927 rebranded as North Hollywood to borrow some glamour from over the hill. Amelia Earhart lived here, the Television Academy settled here, and the old downtown reinvented itself as the NoHo Arts District when the subway arrived in 2000.

3 min read 8 milestones 3 chapters 4 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1886

A Southern Pacific depot opens here under the name Toluca.

- 1887

The Lankershim Ranch Land and Water Company lays out the town of Toluca.

- 1896

The post office takes the name Lankershim.

- 1927

On August 15, Lankershim officially becomes North Hollywood.

- 1934

Amelia Earhart and her husband move to Valley Spring Lane in the Toluca Lake area.

- 1950s

Valley Plaza claims to be the largest shopping center on the West Coast.

- 1981

The North Hollywood library is renamed for Amelia Earhart.

- 2000

The Metro Red Line, now the B Line, opens its North Hollywood terminus.

IThree names

### Toluca, Lankershim, North Hollywood

**1927** the North Hollywood name is adopted

The town began around a Southern Pacific depot called Toluca and was laid out in 1887 by the Lankershim Ranch Land and Water Company. The Lankershim name won out in the 1890s after a local feud. Then in 1927, hoping to capitalize on the movie industry next door, the town renamed itself North Hollywood, and a housing boom followed. The old depot still stands across from the subway station.

II1934

### Amelia Earhart's neighborhood

**1981** the library takes her name

In 1934 Amelia Earhart and her husband, publisher George Putnam, rented a house on Valley Spring Lane and later bought one down the street. She was living here when she set out on her final flight in 1937. The regional library on Tujunga Avenue was renamed in her honor in 1981, beside a monument in North Hollywood Park.

IIINoHo

### The Arts District

**2000** the subway arrives

After the Valley's big malls drew shoppers away, the Lankershim business district emptied out. Small theaters, galleries and studios moved into the low rents, and the area was branded the NoHo Arts District. When the subway reached North Hollywood in 2000, new apartments and offices followed, and the Television Academy's headquarters anchors the district.

The rules here

- **Jurisdiction:** City of Los Angeles
- **Transfer tax:** 0.45% city + 0.11% county
- **Measure ULA:** Applies Yes. 4% of the full price over $5.4M, 5.5% at $10.9M and up (2026 thresholds)
- **Rent control:** LA's Rent Stabilization Ordinance covers most apartments in buildings built before October 1, 1978
- **Public schools:** Los Angeles Unified (LAUSD)

The story of Reseda

## Marian, Reseda and the real epicenter

Reseda began in 1912 as Marian, a farm town named for Marian Otis Chandler, daughter of the Los Angeles Times publisher. It took the name of a flowering plant in 1921 when its new post office needed one, grew into a postwar suburb, and in 1994 turned out to be the true epicenter of the Northridge earthquake.

3 min read 7 milestones 3 chapters 2 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1909

The Los Angeles Suburban Homes Company buys the valley floor and plans its towns.

- 1912

The farm town of Marian appears, named for Marian Otis Chandler.

- 1921

Needing a post office, the town takes the name Reseda, after a fragrant plant.

- 1929

Reseda Avenue becomes Reseda Boulevard in May.

- 1950s

Postwar tracts fill the fields with ranch houses.

- 1984

The Karate Kid is filmed in and around Reseda.

- 1994

At 4:31 a.m. on January 17, a magnitude 6.7 earthquake strikes. The epicenter is just west of Reseda Boulevard, between Arminta and Ingomar streets.

I1912

### A town named Marian

**1921** Marian becomes Reseda

The syndicate that bought the Valley in 1909 planned a string of farm towns, and one of them was named Marian after the daughter of Times publisher Harrison Gray Otis. When the town needed a post office in 1921, the name had to change, and residents chose Reseda, the Latin name of mignonette, a fragrant plant.

IIJanuary 17, 1994

### The Northridge earthquake that started in Reseda

**6.7** magnitude of the 1994 earthquake

The earthquake that struck at 4:31 a.m. on January 17, 1994 was first reported near Northridge, and the name stuck. Seismologists later pinpointed the epicenter just west of Reseda Boulevard, between Arminta and Ingomar streets, in Reseda. It was one of the costliest natural disasters in American history, and it reshaped California's building codes and earthquake insurance.

IIIOn screen

### Suburbia for the movies

**1984** The Karate Kid

With its ranch houses, apartment courts and wide boulevards, Reseda has stood in for American suburbia in many films, most famously The Karate Kid in 1984. Its big lots and flat streets have made it a favorite of builders and investors adding ADUs.

The story of Sherman Oaks

## General Sherman's thousand acres

When a syndicate of Los Angeles power brokers bought most of the southern San Fernando Valley in 1909, streetcar builder Moses Sherman kept 1,000 acres for himself. In 1927 he subdivided them, selling land for about $780 an acre, and the town took his name. Half a century later a shopping mall at Ventura and Sepulveda made Sherman Oaks the capital of Valley culture.

3 min read 7 milestones 2 chapters 2 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1909

The Los Angeles Suburban Homes Company buys 47,500 acres of the southern Valley.

- 1911

Moses Sherman keeps about 1,000 acres around today's Ventura and Sepulveda for himself.

- 1915

The Valley joins Los Angeles for aqueduct water.

- 1927

Sherman subdivides his land and the community of Sherman Oaks is founded.

- 1980

The Sherman Oaks Galleria opens on October 30.

- 1982

The Galleria stars in Fast Times at Ridgemont High.

- 1994

The Northridge earthquake damages the Galleria, which later closes and is rebuilt as an open-air center in 2002.

I1909 to 1927

### The syndicate and the general

**$780** per acre in 1927

In 1909 a syndicate that included Los Angeles Times publisher Harrison Gray Otis, his son-in-law Harry Chandler and streetcar builder Moses Sherman bought 47,500 acres of the Valley and laid out towns and boulevards. Sherman kept about 1,000 acres for himself and in 1927 subdivided them as Sherman Oaks. The street names still read like a list of the partners: Sherman Way, Chandler Boulevard and Hazeltine Avenue, named for Sherman's daughter.

II1980

### The Galleria

**1980** the Galleria opens

The Sherman Oaks Galleria opened in 1980 on the corner where Sherman's original holdings sat, and it quickly became the center of Valley teenage life, immortalized in Fast Times at Ridgemont High in 1982. The 1994 Northridge earthquake damaged it badly, and it was rebuilt as an open-air center that reopened in 2002.

The story of Studio City

## The town named after a movie lot

Studio City is the only neighborhood in Los Angeles named after a studio. Comedy producer Mack Sennett opened a lot here in 1928 and the surrounding tract took its name. The lot became Republic Pictures, then CBS Studio Center, then Radford Studio Center, and in November 2026 Netflix bought it. Down the road sits the adobe site where the fighting for California ended.

3 min read 8 milestones 3 chapters 3 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1847

On January 13, John C. Fremont and Andres Pico sign the Treaty of Cahuenga at the Campo de Cahuenga, ending the fighting in California.

- 1858

The Campo becomes a stop on the Butterfield stage line.

- 1928

Mack Sennett opens his studio at Ventura and Radford with a gala and, reportedly, the world's largest pie.

- 1935

Several small studios merge into Republic Pictures and take over the lot.

- 1963

CBS leases the studio. It buys the lot in 1967 and names it CBS Studio Center.

- 1960s

Gunsmoke, Gilligan's Island and other CBS series are filmed on the lot.

- 2021

CBS's parent sells the lot to Hackman Capital, which renames it Radford Studio Center.

- 2026

Netflix buys the lot for $380 million in November.

I1847

### Where California changed hands

**1847** the Treaty of Cahuenga

Near the mouth of the Cahuenga Pass stood an adobe ranch house where, on January 13, 1847, U.S. Lt. Col. John C. Fremont and Mexican Gen. Andres Pico signed the Treaty of Cahuenga, ending the fighting in California during the Mexican-American War. The adobe later served the Butterfield stagecoach line and was torn down in 1900. Its foundations lie under a small park on Lankershim Boulevard across from Universal, where the signing is reenacted every January.

II1928

### Sennett's studio city

**1928** the Sennett studio opens

Mack Sennett, the producer behind the Keystone Kops, opened a new studio at Ventura Boulevard and Radford Avenue in 1928, and the developers of the land around it named their tract Studio City. Sennett went bankrupt in the Depression, and the lot became Republic Pictures, famous for Westerns and Saturday serials.

IIITV's backyard

### From Republic to Netflix

**$380M** Netflix's 2026 purchase price

CBS moved in during the 1960s, and the lot became the home of Gunsmoke, Gilligan's Island and decades of sitcoms. After a 2021 sale to Hackman Capital for $1.85 billion, the lot was renamed Radford Studio Center, and in November 2026 Netflix bought it for $380 million. A few blocks away, the house on Dilling Street that played the Brady Bunch home is one of the most recognizable houses in television.

The rules here

- **Jurisdiction:** City of Los Angeles
- **Transfer tax:** 0.45% city + 0.11% county

- **Public schools:** Los Angeles Unified (LAUSD)

Real estate

### Netflix buys the Radford Studio Center lot in Studio City for $380 million

The 55-acre, 22-stage lot where Seinfeld and Gunsmoke were filmed drew no bids at Tuesday's foreclosure auction in Pomona, so it went back to the Goldman Sachs-led lenders, and Netflix announced its purchase about an hour later. The price is about a fifth of the $1.85 billion Hackman Capital paid in 2021. ABC7 reports Netflix paid the city's Measure ULA transfer tax on the deal, and the lot will keep running as a working studio.

The story of Tarzana

## Named for Tarzan, by the man who wrote him

Tarzana is the only neighborhood in Los Angeles named after a fictional character. In 1919 Edgar Rice Burroughs, rich from his Tarzan novels, bought the late Los Angeles Times publisher Harrison Gray Otis's country estate, renamed it Tarzana Ranch and began selling lots. When the town got its own post office in 1930, the name went with it.

3 min read 6 milestones 2 chapters 2 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1909

Harrison Gray Otis buys land in the south Valley for his country estate, Mil Flores.

- 1917

Otis dies, and the ranch goes up for sale.

- 1919

On March 1, Edgar Rice Burroughs buys the roughly 540-acre ranch and names it Tarzana Ranch.

- 1920s

Burroughs subdivides and sells much of the land, and a country club leases part of it.

- 1927

Residents petition for their own post office, and Burroughs builds an office on Ventura Boulevard.

- 1930

The Tarzana post office opens on December 12. About 300 people live here.

IMil Flores

### From a publisher's estate to Tarzan's ranch

**1919** Burroughs buys the ranch

Harrison Gray Otis, the publisher of the Los Angeles Times, kept a country estate in the south Valley called Mil Flores, a thousand flowers. After his death it was sold in 1919 to Edgar Rice Burroughs, the Chicago writer whose Tarzan books and movies had made him rich. Burroughs moved his family west, renamed the place Tarzana Ranch, and tried his hand at farming and ranching.

IITarzana

### A town takes the name

**300** residents when the post office opened in 1930

Ranching was expensive, and Burroughs soon began subdividing and selling lots. By the late 1920s a small community had grown up along Ventura Boulevard, and when its post office opened in 1930 it took the ranch's name. Burroughs's company still works from the office he built on Ventura Boulevard in 1927, and he is buried beneath a tree outside it.

Test yourself

### Did you know?

01 **Is Tarzana really named after Tarzan?** Tap for the answer

Yes. Edgar Rice Burroughs named his ranch Tarzana after his famous character, and the town kept the name.

02 **What was the ranch called before Burroughs?** Tap for the answer

Mil Flores, meaning a thousand flowers, the country estate of Los Angeles Times publisher Harrison Gray Otis.

03 **Where is Edgar Rice Burroughs buried?** Tap for the answer

Under a tree outside his company's office on Ventura Boulevard in Tarzana.

The rules here

- **Jurisdiction:** City of Los Angeles
- **Transfer tax:** 0.45% city + 0.11% county
- **Measure ULA:** Applies Yes. 4% of the full price over $5.4M, 5.5% at $10.9M and up (2026 thresholds)
- **Rent control:** LA's Rent Stabilization Ordinance covers most apartments in buildings built before October 1, 1978
- **Public schools:** Los Angeles Unified (LAUSD)

The story of Valley Village

## The neighborhood that named itself

For most of its life, Valley Village was the southwestern corner of North Hollywood. Homeowners began organizing for an identity of their own in 1985, and in 1991 the city put up blue Valley Village signs. Its streets of 1930s and 1940s houses include the block where a young Norma Jean Dougherty lived before she became Marilyn Monroe.

3 min read 6 milestones 2 chapters 1 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1880s

The area is farmland on the Lankershim ranch.

- 1927

The surrounding town renames itself North Hollywood.

- 1944

Norma Jean Dougherty lives with her in-laws in a house on Hermitage Avenue.

- 1985

About 300 homeowners meet at Colfax Avenue Elementary to push for a separate identity.

- 1991

The city installs Valley Village signs.

- 2015

The Hermitage Avenue house is demolished during a fight over its preservation.

I1985 to 1991

### Breaking away from North Hollywood

**1991** Valley Village signs go up

Valley Village was officially part of North Hollywood for decades, although its post office already postmarked mail Valley Village. In December 1985 about 300 homeowners met at Colfax Avenue Elementary to push for their own name and tighter limits on growth. In 1991 the city put up the blue signs, and the name has stuck ever since.

II1944

### Norma Jean on Hermitage Avenue

**1944** Norma Jean lives on Hermitage

During the war, a teenage Norma Jean Dougherty lived with her husband's family in a 1940 house on Hermitage Avenue while he served overseas. Within a few years she was Marilyn Monroe. The house was demolished in 2015 for a condo project while neighbors were still trying to save it, and the fight helped spark a wider preservation effort on the block.

The story of Van Nuys

## The mother of Valley towns

Van Nuys was the first town the Los Angeles Suburban Homes Company built on the Valley floor. It was founded on February 22, 1911, connected to downtown by Red Car before the year was out, joined Los Angeles in 1915 for aqueduct water and spent much of the century building airplanes and Chevrolets.

3 min read 9 milestones 3 chapters 3 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1909

The Los Angeles Suburban Homes Company buys 47,500 acres of the Valley from Isaac Van Nuys and his partners.

- 1911

Van Nuys is founded on February 22. Its first baby, born that October, is named Whitley Van Nuys Huffaker.

- 1911

The Pacific Electric Red Car reaches Van Nuys in December.

- 1915

Van Nuys joins Los Angeles on May 22.

- 1928

Metropolitan Airport opens on December 17, the 25th anniversary of the Wright brothers' first flight.

- 1932

The Van Nuys City Hall tower, now the Valley Municipal Building, is completed.

- 1947

General Motors opens the Van Nuys Assembly plant.

- 1957

The airport takes the name Van Nuys Airport.

- 1992

The GM plant closes in August.

I1911

### A town planned in a year

**Feb. 22, 1911** Van Nuys is founded

The syndicate that bought the Valley in 1909 laid out Van Nuys as its first town, named for Isaac Newton Van Nuys, the rancher whose land they had bought. Lots went on sale in 1911, a hotel and stores went up almost immediately, and the Red Car arrived that December. Four years later, with the aqueduct finished, Van Nuys voted to join Los Angeles.

IIWings and wheels

### Airplanes and Chevrolets

**1947-1992** GM builds cars in Van Nuys

Metropolitan Airport opened in 1928 and became an Army airfield in the Second World War. Workers at a plant there included a young Norma Jean Dougherty, who was photographed on the assembly line before she became Marilyn Monroe. After the war, General Motors built Chevrolets, Camaros and Firebirds at its Van Nuys plant from 1947 to 1992, and Van Nuys Boulevard became famous for weekend cruising. Van Nuys Airport is now one of the busiest general aviation airports in the world.

III1932

### City Hall of the Valley

**1932** the City Hall tower is completed

The white Art Deco tower of the Van Nuys City Hall, completed in 1932, became the civic center of the San Fernando Valley, and the government buildings around it still make Van Nuys the Valley's seat of city business.

December 17, 1928, the 25th anniversary of the Wright brothers' first flight.

03 **What was built at the GM plant?** Tap for the answer

Chevrolets, Camaros and Firebirds, from 1947 to 1992. The site is now The Plant shopping center.

The story of Woodland Hills

## Victor Girard's dream city and Harry Warner's ranch

Woodland Hills began as Girard, a 1922 subdivision by a flamboyant promoter named Victor Girard Kleinberger, who built false storefronts and a mosque-style tower to lure buyers and planted thousands of trees. His company failed, the trees grew, and in 1941 the town renamed itself for them. To the north, a movie mogul's horse ranch later became Warner Center.

3 min read 8 milestones 3 chapters 3 landmarks

### Timeline

- 1922

Victor Girard Kleinberger buys 2,886 acres and lays out the town of Girard, about 6,000 lots.

- 1923

Girard builds gates, a mosque-style tower and a row of false-front stores to impress buyers.

- 1920s

Thousands of trees are planted along the new streets.

- 1940s

Harry Warner of Warner Bros. assembles a horse ranch of about 1,100 acres north of Ventura Boulevard.

- 1941

Residents rename the community Woodland Hills.

- 1947

Pierce College opens as an agricultural school, with a working farm.

- 1967

The Warner family donates 20 acres for Warner Center Park as the ranch is planned into Warner Center.

- 2020

On September 6, Pierce College records 121 degrees, the hottest temperature ever measured in LA County.

I1922

### Girard

**6,000** lots in the original town of Girard

Victor Girard Kleinberger was a salesman with big ideas. In 1922 he bought nearly 2,900 acres of rolling grassland in the southwest Valley and divided it into about 6,000 lots. To make the empty land look like a town, he built entry gates, a tower in a Middle Eastern style and a row of false storefronts along Ventura Boulevard, and he planted thousands of trees. The Depression sank his company. The trees survived.

II1941

### A town named for its trees

**1941** Girard becomes Woodland Hills

By 1941 the trees had grown into the canopy that still shades the older streets, and residents voted to rename the community Woodland Hills. North of Ventura Boulevard, Harry Warner raised thoroughbreds on a ranch of about 1,100 acres. In the 1960s it was planned into Warner Center, now the west Valley's business district, and the family gave 20 acres for a park.

IIIPierce

### A college with a farm

**121°F** LA County's record high, at Pierce in 2020

Pierce College opened in 1947 as an agricultural school and still runs a working farm with animals and fields in the middle of the suburbs. Its weather station holds Los Angeles County's all-time heat record, 121 degrees on September 6, 2020.

# Prop TE: Palisades fire sellers can skip LA's mansion tax | Nathaniel Grivas

Source page: https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/guide/prop-te-palisades-mansion-tax-exemption

[Local LA](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods) / [Articles](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/#articles) / Laws & Money

# Prop TE: Palisades fire sellers can skip LA's mansion tax

By [Nathaniel Grivas](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/about), REALTOR®
November 25, 2026

Proposition TE passed with about 61% of the vote in the latest count, and the county certifies results by November 27. For homeowners in Pacific Palisades who lost a house or had one damaged in the January 2025 fire, it removes Measure ULA from the sale.

## Who qualifies

The exemption covers residential property damaged or destroyed in the Palisades Fire, sold by the person who owned it on January 7, 2025, the day the fire started. The window runs through January 6, 2030, five years from the fire.

- **Qualifies:** the January 2025 owner selling a fire-damaged house or a burned lot before January 6, 2030.
- **Still pays ULA:** anyone who bought after the fire and resells, sales after the five-year window, and property the fire didn't damage.

LAist's voter guide describes the measure as a one-time refund or exemption. If you already closed a fire-damaged sale and paid ULA, ask the city's Office of Finance whether you can get it back.

## What it saves

Take a burned lot in the Palisades that sells for $6,000,000:

- **Without Prop TE:** 4% ULA on the full price is $240,000, plus about $33,600 in regular city and county transfer tax. Total: about $273,600.
- **With Prop TE:** about $33,600. The regular 0.45% city and 0.11% county taxes still apply.

That's $240,000 back in the seller's pocket on one sale. Above $10.9M the ULA rate is 5.5%, so the savings grow with the price.

## What it means for the market

Original owners can now sell a lot at its real value without the price band near $5.4M working against them. Expect more Palisades lots to trade, and expect buyers to ask whether the seller is the January 2025 owner, since that decides whether ULA is in the deal.

Malibu homes that burned were never subject to ULA, because Malibu is its own city. Brentwood and the rest of the City of LA still pay ULA as usual.

## Before you list

Confirm three things: that you owned the property on January 7, 2025, that the property is on record as fire damaged, and that the sale can close before January 6, 2030. Then run the numbers in the [transfer tax calculator](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/transfer-tax/?city=los-angeles&price=6000000) with and without the exemption.

This is general information, not tax or legal advice. Confirm your eligibility with the City of Los Angeles and your CPA or attorney.

**Sources:** [LAist voter guide to Proposition TE](https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/laist-los-angeles-city-voter-game-plan-proposition-te-november-2026-election-guide); [Daily Bruin, November 15, 2026 results](https://dailybruin.com/2026/11/15/la-voters-set-to-approve-all-local-measures-bringing-infrastructure-tax-changes/); [City Clerk, Proposition TE text](https://cityclerk.lacity.org/election/Measure_TE.pdf); [NBC Los Angeles](https://www.nbclosangeles.com/news/local/pacific-palisades-measure-ula/3925737/). # The 90210 homes that pay LA's mansion tax | Nathaniel Grivas

Source page: https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/guide/90210-beverly-hills-post-office-city-of-la

[Local LA](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods) / [Articles](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/#articles) / Laws & Money

# The 90210 homes that pay LA's mansion tax

By [Nathaniel Grivas](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/about), REALTOR®
November 25, 2026

The hills above Beverly Hills, from Coldwater Canyon to Benedict Canyon and Franklin Canyon, use the 90210 ZIP code. They're in the City of Los Angeles. Locals call the area Beverly Hills Post Office, or BHPO, after the post office that delivers its mail.

The ZIP decides where your mail goes. The city line decides your taxes, your schools and your building rules.

## What changes at the city line

- **Transfer tax:** Beverly Hills charges no city transfer tax, only the county's 0.11%. BHPO pays the City of LA's 0.45% plus Measure ULA on sales above $5.4M.
- **Schools:** Beverly Hills homes feed into Beverly Hills Unified. BHPO homes are in LAUSD.
- **City services:** Beverly Hills has its own police and fire departments. BHPO is covered by LAPD and LAFD.
- **Building rules:** BHPO falls under LA's Baseline Hillside Ordinance, which limits how big you can build on a hillside lot.

## The $267,000 example

Two homes sell for $6,000,000 each, one in the Beverly Hills flats and one up the canyon in BHPO:

- **Beverly Hills:** county transfer tax of about $6,600. That's it.
- **BHPO:** about $6,600 county, $27,000 City of LA, and $240,000 in ULA. Total: about $273,600.

Same ZIP, same price, $267,000 apart. Buyers pricing a BHPO home against Beverly Hills comps should know which side of the line each comp sits on, and sellers near $5.4M should price with ULA in mind.

## Other ZIPs that cross city lines

Other ZIPs cross city lines too. 90069 and 90046 cover parts of both West Hollywood and the City of LA, and 90048 splits between West Hollywood and Beverly Grove. A mailing address that says "Los Angeles" or "Beverly Hills" tells you the post office, so check the parcel itself. LA's [ZIMAS](https://zimas.lacity.org/) shows whether an address is in the City of LA.

See how every city on the Westside handles taxes, rent control and schools in [LA isn't one city](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/la-rules).

**Sources:** [LA County Registrar-Recorder, documentary transfer tax rates by city](https://www.lavote.gov/home/records/property-document-recording/documentary-transfer-taxes); [City of Los Angeles Office of Finance, Measure ULA](https://finance.lacity.gov/faq/measure-ula); [ZIMAS](https://zimas.lacity.org/). Dollar figures are calculated from the published rates.

# Measure ULA in 2026: what LA's mansion tax actually costs a seller | Nathaniel Grivas

Source page: https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/guide/measure-ula-mansion-tax-2026

[Local LA](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods) / [Articles](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/neighborhoods/#articles) / Laws & Money

# Measure ULA in 2026: what LA's mansion tax actually costs a seller

By [Nathaniel Grivas](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/about), REALTOR®
November 25, 2026

If you own a home in the City of Los Angeles worth anywhere near $5 million, Measure ULA is the number that decides your net. Here is how it works for sales closing now, with the math most people skip.

## The 2026 thresholds

For sales closing on or after July 1, 2026, the City of Los Angeles charges:

- **$5.4M or less:** no ULA tax
- **More than $5.4M and under $10.9M:** 4% of the full sale price
- **$10.9M or more:** 5.5% of the full sale price

That sits on top of the regular transfer taxes every LA sale pays: 0.45% to the city and 0.11% to the county. The thresholds move up every July 1 with inflation, so check the current numbers before you price.

## ULA works like a cliff

With income tax, a higher rate only touches the dollars above each line. With ULA, crossing $5.4M by one dollar puts the 4% on the entire price.

- **Sell at $5,400,000:** about $30,240 in city and county transfer tax, no ULA. You net roughly $5,369,760 before other costs.
- **Sell at $5,500,000:** $220,000 in ULA plus about $30,800 in regular transfer tax. You net roughly $5,249,200.

Selling for $100,000 more leaves you about $120,000 worse off.

## The dead zone

Run the numbers forward and there's a price band where a higher offer nets you less than a $5.4M sale:

- **Around $5.4M:** a sale has to reach roughly**$5.63M** just to net what $5.4M nets.
- **Around $10.9M:** a sale has to reach roughly**$11.07M** to net what a sale just under $10.9M nets.

Those figures cover transfer taxes only, before commissions and other closing costs. If your home's real value sits inside one of those bands, pricing strategy matters more than almost anything else you do.

## Where it applies

ULA only applies inside the City of Los Angeles. On the Westside and in the Valley that includes neighborhoods like Brentwood, Westwood, Mar Vista, Venice, Pacific Palisades, Los Feliz, Encino, and Sherman Oaks. Separate cities like Beverly Hills and Santa Monica are outside it, though they set their own transfer taxes. The mailing address can say "Los Angeles" even when the property sits in another city, and the reverse, so check the city line on the parcel before you assume.

## Who pays it

In LA, sellers customarily pay the transfer taxes, but it's a negotiable term in the purchase contract. On a sale near a threshold, who covers it becomes part of the negotiation.

## What changed in 2026

- A statewide initiative that could have rolled ULA back was withdrawn in June 2026, so the tax stays as written.
- The City Council declined to put an exemption for new apartment construction on the ballot.
- LA voters approved Proposition TE on November 3, 2026, with about 61% voting yes in the latest count. It exempts residential properties damaged or destroyed in the January 2025 Palisades Fire from ULA when the January 2025 owner sells within five years of the fire. The county certifies results by November 27. More in [what Prop TE means for Palisades sellers](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/guide/prop-te-palisades-mansion-tax-exemption).

## If you're anywhere near the line

Pull your parcel, confirm the city, and price against net proceeds instead of the headline number. The [transfer tax calculator](https://www.nathanielgrivas.com/tools/transfer-tax) shows the cliff for any price. A sale at $5.4M can beat a sale at $5.6M, and buyers near the line know it too.

This is general information, not tax or legal advice. Talk to your CPA or attorney about your specific sale.
